skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: {"id": "ced7d93c-4593-4d8c-bb0c-7aac5b2fb2cb", "value": "Tumulus on pavement from which corridor emerges before curving back to form enclosures; tumulus at edge of monument, at narrow end. Bears some resemblance to Keyhole monuments but some key systematic differences. Goulets have a single perimeter that curves back towards the narrow end of the monument in two parallel lines, giving the appearance of two \u2018wings\u2019. Type 1 goulets have a narrow end and a wide end, with the former being located nearer the tumulus or platform."}

{"id": "5bd35f0a-8424-465d-806b-131d96fb88f4", "value": "(11.7 kya) In the Senegambia the Middle Stone Age appears to have taken place later than in surrounding areas spanning from Marine Isotope Stage (MIS 6) to the Holocene with some sites being as recent as 11.7 kya. It is characterized by the presence of small Levallois flakes and cores as well as axes denticulates points and scrapers made from chert and limestone.4The occurrence of MSA sites is geographically widespread but deposits tend to cluster along rivers including the Senegal River Valley the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 Valley the Dakar Region the Tiemassas area the Gambia Valley and the K\u00e9dougou region as well as northern Guinea-Bissau. As with earlier periods no faunal or human remains survive so it is not known if the MSA populations were archaic human groups Homo sapiens or both. The occurrence of MSA sites is geographically widespread but deposits tend to cluster along rivers including the Senegal River Valley the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 Valley the Dakar Region the Tiemassas area the Gambia Valley and the K\u00e9dougou region47 as well as northern GuineaBissau. The quality of the published research on this period varies enormously from"}

{"id": "d484b8db-665c-4e4c-803e-9026122cc28b", "value": "The closing stages of the Pleistocene Ice Age when the glaciers had begun their final retreat."}

{"id": "9236279d-2969-4db9-b0ca-2f55d9cd3dd0", "value": "This category comprises areas with surface water, either impounded in the form of ponds, lakes and reservoirs or flowing as streams, rivers, and canals etc"}

{"id": "d49040f9-3ac9-4894-a5ce-58048c18e923", "value": "Cette cat\u00e9gorie comprend les zones o\u00f9 l'on trouve des eaux de surface, soit retenues sous forme d'\u00e9tangs, de lacs et de r\u00e9servoirs, soit s'\u00e9coulant sous forme de ruisseaux, de rivi\u00e8res et de canaux, etc."}
{"id": "b1e1c1fe-c80f-4f43-8db9-c331a877913b", "value": "A group of graves or a large cemetery where funerary buildings/monuments are gathered - UNESCO"}
{"id": "f7907e88-5948-4eb4-a104-007a3ca1a8b4", "value": "Groupe de s\u00e9pultures ou grand cimeti\u00e8re o\u00f9 sont rassembl\u00e9s des \u00e9difices/monuments fun\u00e9raires."}

{"id": "0faa13db-ed53-473b-9356-10c06eafc478", "value": "A structure with a square or triangular base and sloping straight or stepped sides that meet at the top in a point, normally monumental and usually made of stone"}

{"id": "c76839a9-802d-427d-82d2-1f4009d4752b", "value": "Une structure avec une base carr\u00e9e ou triangulaire et des c\u00f4t\u00e9s inclin\u00e9s droits ou en escalier qui se rejoignent au sommet en un point, g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement monumental et en pierre"}

{"id": "758cb440-e576-4377-9f5e-3d9187762f75", "value": "~1430 - 1510 centuries (AD): Stoneware/Porcelain decorated with cobalt on a white porcelain body covered with a clear colorless glaze and mostly made in the city of Jingdezhen located on the southern bank of the Chang River in Jiangxi Province. The ware becomes increasingly present in assemblages in Eastern and Southern Africa around the mid 15th Century AD onwards."}

{"id": "450c0f36-9c26-4a31-8a05-42844978e1df", "value": "Zimbabwe period V (AD 1833\u20131900) is characterised by class 5 pottery at Great Zimbabwe and R (rough) type walling. It is suggested to be the youngest of phases identified at Great Zimbabwe."}

{"id": "f923e088-d920-42eb-8a3d-c336970d5e03", "value": "A period associated with the development of social formations synonymous with ranked forms of organisation that appeared south of the Zambezi from the late first millennium AD marked by the construction of stonewalled monumental architecture and the production of surplus food for people living in un urban centres. Description: The Zimbabwe culture famous for its dry-stone-built capitals is arguably one of the most important cultural developments in the last two millennia of sub-Saharan prehistory/history | From about AD 1000 - 1200."}

{"id": "2d53a5d5-d224-47d4-b628-554580fad53f", "value": "General: By about 1270 a wealthy elite had emerged at Great Zimbabwe which laid the foundations of an elaborate urban complex and the centre of a state constructing stone buildings of unparalleled scale and magnitude from about 1300 (Garlake 1973). For the next 150 years Great Zimbabwe became the dominant political authority south of the Zambezi (Huffman 1996 2007). Great Zimbabwe reached its peak during the 14th and 15th centuries when elaborate stone walling that symbolized wealth power and status was extended towards outlying areas. With an estimated population of nearly 20000 Great Zimbabwe was the largest metropolis in southern Africa. Ceramics: Incisions graphite burnishing occasional polychrome. Architecture: Freestanding walls occasional terraces. Date: AD 1200\u2013AD 1550"}

{"id": "fd4ffb2a-4829-4b94-b7b9-d0895dcb7498", "value": "A period associated with the development of social formations synonymous with ranked forms of organisation that appeared south of the Zambezi from the late first millennium AD marked by the construction of stonewalled monumental architecture and the production of surplus food for people living in un urban centres. Description: The Zimbabwe culture famous for its dry-stone-built capitals is arguably one of the most important cultural developments in the last two millennia of sub-Saharan prehistory/history | From about AD 1000 - 1200."}

{"id": "acceac3c-008d-4555-b17a-397addbeb1ff", "value": "Zimbabwe III is associated with the earliest evidence of stone walling with no clear courses and pottery that is rarely decorated. It is thought to have evolved out of Gumanye. The makers of Zimbabwe III pottery are thought to be ancestors to Shona-speakers in southern Africa."}

{"id": "a0bc4f8c-bf08-4a25-8da3-b6f5b7bfcaf2", "value": "Refers to the last of the Zimbabwe Culture type walling. Walls are built of undressed blocks and have no courses. Often identified with the Refuge period and Zimbabwe Period V. The chronology of stone walling was developed by Summers Robinson and Whitty (1961) for the site of Great Zimbabwe.The use of P Q and R-type walling as a chronological indicator is debated."}

{"id": "18fc3358-2ae3-4fc4-a659-bb9d0b2d347b", "value": "Earliest walling with no clear courses and flourished between AD 1085 and 1450. Chronology of different types of walling at the site of Great Zimbabwe was developed by Summers Robinson and Whitty (1961) and suggested to be part of Zimbabwe period III and associated with class 3 ceramics."}

{"id": "a9cf4140-ab63-481d-a652-68f963e8e079", "value": "Refers to a second class of walling identified at Zimbabwe culture sites. Walling was built with clear courses (neatly coursed) that can be traced over long distance and built with dressed blocks of a regular size and shape. The chronology of the different styles of walling for Zimbabwe culture sites was based at Great Zimbabwe by Summers Robinson and Whitty (1961). Authors attributed this style of walling to Zimbabwe period IV and lasted from AD 1450 until 1833.The use of P Q and R-type walling as a chronological indicator is debated."}
{"id": "34dc2403-35e4-461c-9bb4-92a48c355372", "value": "Site dont les activit\u00e9s se rapportent \u00e0 la production, l\u2019utilisation et la consommation des biens mat\u00e9riels"}
{"id": "339a203f-847b-4b1c-87f0-d90a3503cc0e", "value": "Site whose activities relate to the production, use and consumption of material goods."}

{"id": "3aa1bda3-c8e6-4c4b-b773-830a599356be", "value": "Major rim classes: SC LC carinated ledged SCL2 SO vertical E1a E2 E3 Major twines: Tw4 Tw5 twisted twines braided twines tiny \u2018swoosh\u2019 CWS knotted cord Major decorations: Incision comb-dragging pin incision fish-vertebrae rouletting punctate stamping appliqu\u00e9d cordons multiple decoration rare carved roulette Paste characteristics: Sandy gritty paste medium to medium-fine texture occasional airy pasted fabric sand- shell- organic- or grog-tempered Color range: Pale orange dark orange red light brown brown grey black Characteristic vessel forms: 1) Beveled open bowl or plate 2) Open bowl twine decoration 3) Short-collared oblique jar slipped rim and twine below collar or multiple decoration involving (slipping wavy comb-dragging incisions appliqu\u00e9d dots or cordon twine or fish-vertebrae roulettes 4) Long-collared oblique jars slipped rim and twine below collar 5) Carinated jars burnished (sometimes reduced) slip"}

{"id": "9568055d-f7b8-4533-894f-bf77a5177f67", "value": "Major rim classes: E4 E5 E6 E7 E9 SCL2 SO possible SC Twine: Tw6 Tw7 Tw4 Tw5 braided twines split-stick cord-wrapped stick Decorations: Slip incisions (crosshatching zigzag chevron) fingernail impressions punctates fish-vertebrae rouletting appliqu\u00e9d cordons Paste characteristics: Medium-coarse (granular paste) to medium-fine sand- grog- or shelltempered Color range: Buff off-white light pink pale orange dark orange light brown Characteristic vessel forms: 1) Jar with long everted lips plain slipped rim (interior and exterior) or twine decoration (interior lip below rim) 2) Wide-everted jar with flat or beveled lip deep-red or orange slipped rim (interior and exterior) 3) Closed or collared oblique jar slip twine incisions punctates or appliqu\u00e9d (below rim) 4) Open bowl plain"}

{"id": "a3a28ba4-4525-4246-8b13-64b420f073bf", "value": "In Senegal the Iron Age coincides with the period of invention and development of metallurgical techniques between 2000 BC and 1600 AD. The period is also known for its regional diversity in the type of material culture identified. This has allowed archaeologists to divide the period according to the different site and material markers from megaliths habitat sites tumuli to shell mounds. | The habitat sites are flattened mounds with little relief (2-5 m high) and can be grouped or isolated. Their extremely variable extents extend over several hundred meters in length and width and are sometimes covered with shards of pottery the remains of metallurgical activity (slag tuy\u00e8res) and various debris. The phenomenon of habitat sites extends without interruption from Dagana to nearly 200 km south of Bakel in a vast space between the fossilized hydrographic network of the Ferlo in the south and the Senegal River valley in the north. Elsewhere these sites are also found in the Sine-Saloum and in the south towards Kolda. | Major rim classes: SO SCL2 Twine: Multiple-stick cord-wrapped stick possible Tw6 Decorations: Plain incisions fingernail impressions Paste characteristics: Undetermined Characteristic vessel forms: Closed ovoid jar and Open globular bowl."}

{"id": "20c08408-5b57-4eb5-8e2e-3ec57445c954", "value": "Major rim classes: SCL2 SCL1 SO some carinated and collared rims Major twines: Tw4 Tw5 Tw6 tiny \u2018swoosh\u2019 CWS knotted cord Decorations: Slipping incisions comb-channeling Paste characteristics: Sandy gritty paste well-consolidated medium-fine with occasional medium texture sand- and grog-tempered Color range: light-brown pale orange buff pale pink dark orange brown generally dark-cored Characteristic vessel forms: 1) Closed oblique jar slipped rim groove and twine 2) Closed oblique jar Twine field and overlapping incisions 3) Open bowl slipping twine or comb-channeling"}

{"id": "55c2dabc-6310-4550-9045-481a1b76b7a3", "value": "Major rim classes: E3 E4 E5 E6 SC SCL2 some LC carinated Major decorations: Tw4 Tw5 Tw6 braided twines knotted cord Paste characteristics: Sandy gritty paste wide variation in texture and firing Color range: Pale orange dark orange light brown brown Characteristic vessel forms: 1) Jar with everted lip slip or twine-impressions (interior rim and exterior) 2) Collared oblique jars fish-vertebrae roulette multiple twine decoration or twine-incision combination 3) Closed ovoid jar slipped rim."}

{"id": "dbb3b546-019c-4a4b-bec4-f6733e3c1b1e", "value": "In Senegal the Iron Age coincides with the period of invention and development of metallurgical techniques between 2000 BC and 1600 AD. The period is also known for its regional diversity in the type of material culture identified. This has allowed archaeologists to divide the period according to the different site and material markers from megaliths habitat sites tumuli to shell mounds. | The habitat sites are flattened mounds with little relief (2-5 m high) and can be grouped or isolated. Their extremely variable extents extend over several hundred meters in length and width and are sometimes covered with shards of pottery the remains of metallurgical activity (slag tuy\u00e8res) and various debris. The phenomenon of habitat sites extends without interruption from Dagana to nearly 200 km south of Bakel in a vast space between the fossilized hydrographic network of the Ferlo in the south and the Senegal River valley in the north. Elsewhere these sites are also found in the Sine-Saloum and in the south towards Kolda. | Major rim classes: SO SCL2 Twine: Multiple-stick cord-wrapped stick possible Tw6 Decorations: Plain incisions fingernail impressions Paste characteristics: Undetermined Characteristic vessel forms: Closed ovoid jar and Open globular bowl."}

{"id": "0437929b-07d2-4bc8-837e-15fdc205081b", "value": "An individual designated by the museum director to have primary responsibility for the preservation, care and maintenance of museum property and providing guided tours to heritage/archaeological sites."}

{"id": "efe9e9c5-5a37-487b-92ed-7eed963c8393", "value": "Personne d\u00e9sign\u00e9e par le directeur du mus\u00e9e pour assumer la responsabilit\u00e9 principale de la pr\u00e9servation, de l'entretien et de la maintenance des biens du mus\u00e9e, ainsi que des visites guid\u00e9es des sites patrimoniaux/arch\u00e9ologiques."}

{"id": "ede92902-639e-450d-8eee-6cb8ec87bc44", "value": "An individual who is not directly working for a national heritage body/museum but reports the existence of a heritage site in their area to the museum"}

{"id": "45d6e1bb-f48b-4edb-94ac-c29227ab7e76", "value": "Une personne qui ne travaille pas directement pour un organisme/mus\u00e9e du patrimoine national, mais qui signale au mus\u00e9e l'existence d'un site patrimonial dans sa r\u00e9gion."}
{"id": "9188ceff-eb23-4d8d-9cd8-97b7fa61c4e2", "value": "An institute which carries out academic research but which is not a university or part of a university (e.g. has little or no teaching)"}

{"id": "1162b4dc-169d-4eb5-8418-5f390c6445e9", "value": "Un institut qui effectue des recherches acad\u00e9miques mais qui n'est pas une universit\u00e9 ou une partie d'une universit\u00e9 (par exemple, qui n'enseigne pas ou peu)."}
{"id": "54dc2c27-80aa-4464-b73f-38a5d9cacbcf", "value": "A researcher who is not part of the direct MAEASaM team or the collaborating institutions"}
{"id": "23209785-ed36-4de4-82d4-5a6290cb6b56", "value": "Un chercheur qui ne fait pas partie de l'\u00e9quipe directe de MAEASaM ou des institutions collaboratrices"}

{"id": "cb60808e-a0a5-47f8-8098-fdbd70e0eab9", "value": "Une institution qui conserve et expose des objets consid\u00e9r\u00e9s d'int\u00e9r\u00eat public en raison de leur valeur historique, culturelle, scientifique ou artistique."}

{"id": "9c8500ae-5ed0-45d8-a36a-440c18e73a53", "value": "An institution which stores and exhibits items considered to be of public interest due to their historical, cultural, scientific, or artistic value"}
{"id": "ac0e4d54-f818-442a-91c7-6b280fa40154", "value": "Une personne qui \u00e9tudie dans une universit\u00e9 ou un autre \u00e9tablissement d'enseignement sup\u00e9rieur, ou un \u00e9colier."}
{"id": "522c2784-5976-4408-ab81-05442843a03a", "value": "A person who is studying at a university or other place of higher education or a school pupil"}
{"id": "a666dd7f-660d-4783-8333-86e72fd30375", "value": "Un \u00e9tablissement d'enseignement sup\u00e9rieur qui dispense des cours aux \u00e9tudiants et effectue de la recherche."}
{"id": "c676c6cc-544a-42ed-bfed-c5827c3f5a23", "value": "A place of higher education which both teaches students and carries out research"}
{"id": "4547e3ce-3d1e-4d97-8326-98a97d719f80", "value": "Une personne qui travaille directement pour l'\u00e9quipe MAEASaM ou qui a travaill\u00e9 pour elle dans le pass\u00e9."}
{"id": "550a1048-c8d1-4ff3-a334-3d4925d625ad", "value": "A person who is working directly for the MAEASaM team, or who has worked for them in the past"}
{"id": "f54d3302-8272-4aaa-93a6-ab751b4731e5", "value": "An institution or individual that can be regarded as a shareholder in the heritage site, but does not form part of the government structure"}

{"id": "c0416bf3-2c49-419d-983c-7e1e4ab363a3", "value": "Une institution ou un individu qui peut \u00eatre consid\u00e9r\u00e9 comme un actionnaire du site patrimonial, mais qui ne fait pas partie de la structure gouvernementale."}
{"id": "d11049af-a488-4d79-a0c9-543130320d11", "value": "Une organisation qui a un but pr\u00e9cis (religieux, \u00e9ducatif, professionnel ou social)."}
{"id": "ee6f9cd3-e811-48b1-96d5-1ef24fb03298", "value": "An organization founded for a specific purpose (religious, educational, professional, or social)"}
{"id": "f4e45226-d2f3-453b-baad-92a4ced14e24", "value": "Une personne ou un service qui fait partie de la structure de l'autorit\u00e9 gouvernante"}
{"id": "2347ab36-4edc-4c35-9f5b-4608248fbecf", "value": "An individual or department that forms part of the governing authority structure"}

{"id": "8e4cf3f7-bc18-4727-aad3-6ef97a7fa879", "value": "Une ou plusieurs personnes repr\u00e9sentant une communaut\u00e9 qui peut \u00eatre consid\u00e9r\u00e9e comme un actionnaire du site patrimonial"}
{"id": "266a638c-987a-4828-904b-fac7674844f0", "value": "An individual/s that represent an community that can be regarded as being a shareholder in the heritage site"}
{"id": "43bca3c6-6ee7-43fd-ae74-a839346eb5bd", "value": "Une personne qui ne travaille pas directement pour l'\u00e9quipe MAEASaM, mais qui travaille pour une institution partenaire du projet."}

{"id": "7c304a65-b963-470d-85d7-4a930ee87f94", "value": "A person who is not working directly for the MAEASaM team, but who works for a partner institution of the project, such as a national heritage body/museum"}

{"id": "01a9f699-f3dc-49d3-ac49-eb0b573ba42e", "value": "The section of a country's government which is responsible for the cultural and historical (and sometimes also natural) heritage within that particular country"}

{"id": "1eee00e8-bd06-4053-b993-cb379bcd31ba", "value": "La section du gouvernement d'un pays qui est responsable du patrimoine culturel et historique (et parfois aussi naturel) dans un pays particulier."}

{"id": "44b074d3-331c-4207-a445-82857b993687", "value": "A person affiliated with the MAEASaM project (and therefore not entirely an external researcher), but who is not either a direct member of the team or a member of a partner institution. Intended as a catch-all - if these other terms are applicable, use them instead."}

{"id": "e09f39ff-2a00-4b74-87a3-444f474f10f5", "value": "Une personne affili\u00e9e au projet MAEASaM (et qui n'est donc pas enti\u00e8rement un chercheur externe), mais qui n'est ni un membre direct de l'\u00e9quipe ni un membre d'une institution partenaire. Il s'agit d'un terme fourre-tout - si ces autres termes sont applicables, utilisez-les \u00e0 la place."}
{"id": "80694747-3d2f-46a3-9689-a077d9b49692", "value": "Une personne ou une organisation qui est actionnaire du site patrimonial mais qui ne correspond \u00e0 aucune des autres cat\u00e9gories."}
{"id": "98f88c6b-ccf3-487c-a231-255fa64fc6c8", "value": "An individual/s or organization that are shareholders in the heritage site but do not match any of the other categories"}

{"id": "8b5a34b2-1685-432f-a360-87b64e6611f7", "value": "Definition 1: Zhizo related settlements nearly doubled by AD 1000 in the Mhalapye-Palapye area of Botswana. An example of a major capital named Toutswemogala Hill developed. Archaeologists have termed the pottery associated with this phase as Toutswe. Earlier Zhizo pottery in the area have been called Taukome. Description: From Schroda and Ratho Farm in the middle Limpopo Valley and extending further west towards the Kalahari margins lineages established ranked societies minimally chiefdoms especially at Toutswemogala Taukome and Bosutswe where sites with Zhizo type pottery attest to increased population and considerable social transformation. It is highly likely that the rst chiefdoms and state societies in southern Africa developed around these sites."}
{"id": "2972e0ac-1cf8-4e82-9092-04a2c186ec00", "value": "The southern group of tumuli is dated between 700 and 1000 AD."}
{"id": "bc88507e-df10-4ce4-a498-a572fe2e0b98", "value": "A watercraft designed to submerge, travel and operate below the water's surface"}
{"id": "efba9e03-5a7a-4918-9a24-4813dd545045", "value": "A linear heritage resource which does not follow a regular/straight, and may incorporate bends and/or curves"}
{"id": "25898fcd-77d0-494f-a72a-3cb975e37b63", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource which is round in shape"}
{"id": "c810b165-8045-40da-967f-b8ad3bdc7c58", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource with one straight side and one curved/rounded side (e.g. D-shaped)"}
{"id": "77034ce2-0ea2-4812-972a-441ea1fc6430", "value": "An enclosed or unenclosed heritage resource with no identifiable geometric form"}
{"id": "dd78ad35-f1c7-4887-b1cd-c9d61c9f225a", "value": "Unknown"}
{"id": "8513b8c7-54ef-4ee7-9a3f-a114d6266bd2", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource which is rectangular in overall shape but with rounded corners or edges"}

{"id": "e2ac1da4-5465-4d5c-a47d-0bce16e09b33", "value": "Any shape which has been drawn to define the edge of area which is being treated as a single 'site' by the researcher for no other reason than the geographical proximity of heritage resources visible on the imagery (e.g. a large area which contains 1000s of cairns, pendants, and small enclosures, when you have no reason to believe that the individual heritage resources are necessarily related functionally or chronologically, but where we do not want to/cannot enter individual records, for reasons of time. If you use this category, your 'Certainty' for 'Site size/extent' should always be 'Negligible'."}
{"id": "c8ef6e8c-d264-4224-8a33-fec7b992a2de", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource which is rounded in shape, but not necessarily circular"}
{"id": "177ecb10-e99b-4a5a-bfa9-33f8b0f6e0a9", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource with 4 straight sides arranged at right angles"}

{"id": "614a7f26-9f74-4202-9581-f9ad4e69b858", "value": "For use only on sites which consist of a single very small findspot which is too small to be recognised on satellite imagery under normal circumstances. e.g. an isolated stone tool with no other objects or features around"}
{"id": "1678a59b-b1f7-4ee0-9d41-c1505cd95347", "value": "A linear heritage resource which bends in alternating directions at intervals"}
{"id": "0538e0ac-7c3a-4405-a37e-84b41611ae21", "value": "An enclosed or unenclosed heritage resource which is formed of straight sides sitting at more or less right angles"}
{"id": "6f0f05ef-5388-4b36-91cc-5b9012968d6e", "value": "A linear heritage resource which curves"}
{"id": "47b3d976-8ea6-4ee1-be6c-2ae9ce93806d", "value": "An enclosed heritage resource of 3 straight sides."}
{"id": "0b252b81-370f-48c7-9f5f-1e7a21becdf1", "value": "A linear heritage resource which does not curve or bend"}

{"id": "28316992-0ea4-4f75-98fb-21e871c9a974", "value": "Any naturally situated rock, boulder, exfoliation, stalagmite or stalactite which resonates when struck and shows evidence of use as an idiophone (i.e. an instrument which vibrates as a whole to produce a sound) - in contrast to other lithophones which are portable, and have been either artificially tuned, or show evidence of being selected for their tonal suitability."}

{"id": "b6a376a5-5acb-4e5c-9683-043a3cb2b96c", "value": "Tout rocher, bloc, exfoliation, stalagmite ou stalactite situ\u00e9 dans la nature, qui r\u00e9sonne lorsqu'on le frappe et qui montre des signes d'utilisation comme idiophone (c'est-\u00e0-dire un instrument qui vibre dans son ensemble pour produire un son) - par opposition \u00e0 d'autres lithophones qui sont portables et qui ont \u00e9t\u00e9 accord\u00e9s artificiellement ou qui montrent des signes de s\u00e9lection pour leur aptitude \u00e0 produire un son."}

{"id": "f860a659-e54e-475e-9cc0-cfdff31c2211", "value": "Dated between 1100 and 950 BC this phase is only present in Diallowalli and is characterized by pottery with simple edges. They are decorated by impressions with braided twisted or folded cord. The incisions and applied decorations are aditive motifs. A bone industry is also found which links the Diallowalli site to that of Khant."}

{"id": "f44fb6b9-429c-4d05-958c-607c17f1c265", "value": "This phase is characterized by accurate black cups with regular rim bands forming rail track patterns and gray black greasy slip. The lithic industry includes flakes from multiple platform cores followed by single and opposite platform cores. There is a widespread use of agate followed by quartz. Perforators are the most common tools."}

{"id": "079159c0-0388-4e85-ae12-577353529616", "value": "This period can be understood as the first appearance of material culture which is connected to the Gash Group. The Proto Gash Group produced rather characteristic sherds: some wiped ware and a fragment of rippled ware. Only a few sherds of this phase were found at Mahal Teglinos. The lithic industry shows a significant percentage of ninety-degree core flakes single platform flakes and geometrics are the most characteristic tools."}

{"id": "9b53ebfa-8ddf-40a1-818c-677a2b858f2d", "value": "The sites of the Gash Group are recorded along the Gash Delta Kassala Province and in the alluvial plains south of it. The main site is Mahal Teglinos (K1). The material culture is dominated by scraped vessels the rest of the ceramics are mostly decorated with rim band designs: simple dash rouletted punctuate zoned and horizontal zig-zag patterns. The flaked stone industry is basically microlithic with a small amount of blades. (Fattovich 1993) | In the Early Phase of the Gash Culture there are some transitional phenomena. Most artefacts were found in the excavations at Shurab el Gash which may be regarded as a transitional Butana/Gash site. The earliest funerary stelae most likely go back to this period. More finds are from Mahal Teglinos and ES 1. The ceramics include bowls decorated with comb impressed bands which often extend to the body of the vessel and/or rim bands made by impression. There are also plain bowls with notches on top of the lip accurately scraped and wiped ware and a vegetal tempered ware. The lithic industry shows a significant percentage of ninety-degree core flakes single platform flakes and geometrics are the most characteristic tools. The subsistence economy includes the keeping of cattle and sheep/goats but hunting and gathering is an important component. With the appearance of elements from Early Kerma and C-Group there is a beginning of trade visible."}

{"id": "81b7f59f-e80a-4359-af36-5a9f228cc7df", "value": "The ceramics include bowls and cups decorated with impressed or incised rim bands patterns of crossed lines forming rim bands decoration which consists of parallel horizontal grooves that get sometimes crossed by grooves called finger nail ware. There is also abundant scraped ware which can be modeled with clay decoration and has often pinched or intdented rims. The lithic assemblage is composed of flakes from multiple platform cores and flint is the favoured raw material. In this period the size of population is the biggest. There are many artefacts which suggest a trade with the peoples of Egypt Sudan Ethiopia and perhaps Somalia and Southern Arabia. Mahal Teglinos is occupied by a large residential village about 10-11 hectares in size and probably it became an important trading city."}

{"id": "e6bcb1f0-df88-4f0c-808a-eea598fd7e90", "value": "The sites of the Gash Group are recorded along the Gash Delta Kassala Province and in the alluvial plains south of it. {"id": "19056546-6a96-438c-a7f3-377576e58f9b", "value": "A period when Swahili coastal towns were established and flourished. The Swahili coast runs for 3000km from Somalia to Mozambique and is composed of more than 450 urban settlements built initially with mud and later with coral and limestone mortar. These 'urban' settlements were surrounded by fortified stone walls. The architecture of these towns shows Asian Arabi and Indian influences while the material artefacts include exotic items from faraway lands such as China. 700-1600CE | Marked by local Early Iron Age pottery iron and iron slag 100BCE-300CE"}

{"id": "7b47242a-d523-4a20-9298-2b3ea0a3ab25", "value": "A period when semi-sedentary agro-pastoralists arrived at the coast and established wattle and daub settlements containing large amounts of Kwale and Tana /TIW wares and evidence of iron production. Settlements such as Shanga Manda and Kilwa were established at this time. 1400-1000BP | Tana ware (also called Early Tana Tradition pottery or Triangular-Incised Ware) refers to a type of pottery produced in East Africa in the late 1st millennium. The presence of this pottery is largely regarded as one of the best indicators for early Swahili settlement and the name Tana was given because the early discoveries of these types of pottery were along the Tana River in present day Kenya. As indicated by the name this pottery features particular type of decoration in the form of triangular incised lines and a single row of dots. and also fingernail pinches parallel horizontal lines shell edge punctuates and a cross hatching on rims. Tana has five main vessel types - necked jars globular jars open bowls closed bowls and carinated bowls. The geographic distribution of this pottery tradition is widespread covering the East African coast from Kenya in the north to Mozambique in the south as well as the central hinterland inland. 600-1000CE | Tana ware (also called Early Tana Tradition pottery or Triangular-Incised Ware) refers to a type of pottery produced in East Africa in the late 1st millennium. {"id": "6905f77a-629b-42b8-bbf4-8e183c3b7087", "value": "The Neogene includes the Miocene and Pliocene epochs (23700000\u20131600000 years ago) and is considered by some to encompass the time up to the present. The Neogene which means newborn was designated as such to emphasize that the marine and terrestrial fossils found in the strata of this time were more closely related to each other than to those of the preceding period called the Paleogen. | On the geologic time scale the youngest epoch of the Tertiary or of the more recently designated Neogene following Miocene and preceding the Pleistocene epoch of the Quaternary period. It extends from about 5.3 million to 2.58 million years ago."}

{"id": "29837164-33f9-4182-b0b3-74afe11d22d9", "value": "The Meroitic period at times also called the Meroitic Dynasty of Kingdom was born from the political consequences of the organisation of the exotic trade between Lower Nubia and Egypt after the latter acquired control over Lower Nubia between the First and Second Cataracts. The Egyptian occupation of Lower Nubia and the organisation of the trade route along the Nile contributed to the development of the settlement chain in the Nile Valley north and south of the Second Cataract. The Meroitic period starting with Arkamaniqo's reign is characterized by a proportionate development of the kingdom as a whole and not only its southern regions. Many changes and developments happened during this period notably the move of the royal burial site from the region of Napata to that of Meroe city and the development of the Meroitic hieroglyphs."}

{"id": "100e1eb3-9b94-484f-95cb-cb7f6d05f1c4", "value": "An industry of that follows and partially overlaps the Southern African and Eastern African Later Stone Age and has three broad phases: Nachikufan 1 (c. 16700 to 10800 BP) Nachikufan 2 (c. 9700--5000 B.P) Nachikufan 3 (c. 3500--200 B.P.). All known Nachikufan sites are found in Zambia. They lie north of the Zambezi river mostly west of the Luangwa river and primarily east of the Kafue river. | Follows and partially overlaps with the Southern and Eastern Africa Later Stone Age tradition and occurs north of the Zambezi River. Nachikufan 1 has been identified as the earliest phase of the Nachikufan industry and is estimated to date between 16700 to 10800 BP."}

{"id": "070d1b1e-1ca9-4c9d-97eb-7df5dec7cc59", "value": "Northern Chinese stonewares made principally in Hopeh Honan Shansi and Shantung provinces between the Sung and Ming dynasties (960-1644 CE). Z'u-chou arose from the tradition of T'ang dynasty (618-906) white wares but coarse local clays required the use of a creamy white slip to mask the dark color of the buff-grey body. This white slip is the distinguishing characteristic of Tz'u-chou ceramics which consisted primarily of inexpensive wares for everyday use. Some basic methods included black-and-brown painting on white slip white or black slip with deeply carved decoration that exposed the clay body (cut-glaze technique) black slip sgraffiato designs on white slip incised and stamped decoration green lead glaze and the earliest use of enamel overglaze decoration. (Porcelain and stoneware)"}

{"id": "999d38f4-0796-4fd5-8fba-0c4cf3584e7e", "value": "15th Century: East African assemblages one sort stands out. It consists of small wound beads most of which are transparent-translucent ruby red and a few that are amber-coloured. They are distinctive not only because small wound beads are rare but the colours are unusual as well. The largest number of them was found at Kilwa\u2019s Husuni Kubwa Tanzania. One example found at Great Zimbabwe. These beads came from contexts dated to around the early 15th century likely origins from China."}

{"id": "bbd6d735-b2ef-4ba4-af89-76ef5473f52f", "value": "\u2018Sgraffiato\u2019 describes the decorative technique of incising linear designs through a white slip before glazingr. In pottery the pattern is incised through a white or coloured slip (mixture of clay and water washed over the vessel before firing) revealing the body colour beneath. Can be plain glazed glazed with floral motif or hatched motif. Sgraffiato is therefore a long-lived and widespread tradition which can be subdivided into a number of lesser traditions with a more limited geographical and chronological range based on the style of decoration fabric and technique of manufacture. Islamic sgraffiato vessels are categorised into early Sgraffiato dating to around 9th - 11th centuries (AD) and late Sgraffiato dating to around the 11th - 13th centuries (AD). By the 12th century the technique had become the most widespread and common of the Islamic ceramic traditions: it is found in Egypt the coast of East Africa Syria Northern Iraq Central Asia and Byzantium and entered the European tradition through Northern Italy in the early 13th century"}

{"id": "32053494-f234-437c-90c8-3532388a0448", "value": "One of the commonest types of imported pottery found around the Indian Ocean in the 7th\u201310th centuries was a large jar commonly known as Sassanian\u2013Islamic ware with Persian Gulf origins. The Sasanian\u2013Islamic ware displayed either a green glaze with modelled swirls ribs and protrusions or a turquoise blue glaze on one side and a light green on the reverse is commonly found along the East African coast."}

{"id": "53da2f24-33fd-41c0-842a-875501c0d0e2", "value": "Description: despite the antiquity of this trade only in the last few centuries BC did it link the area of study [from Middle East to East Asia reaching as far apart as West Africa and the American Pacific coast]. | Description: 7th - 8th Century AD. Based on chemical analysis Chibuene series beads probably came from the Middle East east of the Euphrates with the Sasanian Persian Gulf trade. Possibly found at Nqoma western Botswana and potentially at sites in East Africa. Around the middle-to-late 10th century importation of Zhizo beads ceased and Chibuene\u2019s role as a port serving Indian Ocean trade and the interior of southern Africa ended. These beads are also found at several sites in West Africa beginning in around the 8th century AD but seem to vanish from trade there by the end of the first millennium AD."}

{"id": "7aad6212-7376-489d-bf5d-0167f4c5c2c1", "value": "Starting around the 10th century (AD) Qingbai Ware constitutes the one of the largest categories of Chinese monochrome ceramics most exported into the Muslim world and East Africa between 11th and 13th centuries (AD) all of which has glaze ranging in color from pale blue gray to pale blue and including blue-gray-green and even off-white."}

{"id": "b093f164-65b3-4374-acdd-4e2e39c7882a", "value": "Description: despite the antiquity of this trade only in the last few centuries BC did it link the area of study [from Middle East to East Asia reaching as far apart as West Africa and the American Pacific coast]. | Description: 7th - 8th Century AD. Possibly found at Nqoma western Botswana and potentially at sites in East Africa. Around the middle-to-late 10th century importation of Zhizo beads ceased and Chibuene\u2019s role as a port serving Indian Ocean trade and the interior of southern Africa ended. These beads are also found at several sites in West Africa beginning in around the 8th century AD but seem to vanish from trade there by the end of the first millennium AD."}

{"id": "effc0546-4197-40e1-b2ea-7d249b73dfd2", "value": "900 to 1050 AD: These ceramics have soft pink to pink-buff paste very fine with little temper and smooth fracture. The internal surface is decorated with white glaze and brown colour iridescence. The ware noted to be from Siraf and Susa sites in Iran."}

{"id": "52bd1cd5-9daf-437f-86f9-31cb9b226eb0", "value": "9th to 10th centuries AD: earthen ware with soft white to buff paste with a fine temper and fairly smooth fracture. It consists of undefined areas of green brown and yellow splashes with green often being the predominant colour. Considered to derive from the Persian Gulf region."}

{"id": "53a61c64-082d-48ca-b328-05f58cf72e85", "value": "The term Celadon is today used in at least three different ways as denoting a color a glaze and a ware. Celadon glaze - greenish high-fired and used on top of a white porcelain body. Wares: A term first minted in Europe to describe the wares decorated with a subtle sea green glaze - obtained by slight underfiring - and made at the kilns centered in the Longquan area of southern Zhejiang province Colour: High-fired green wares in general in China known as qingci. Occurs throughout the Indian Ocean network and in Eastern Africa around the early 9th Century (AD) and onwards. | Wares mostly decorated with greenish glaze made at kilns centered in the Longquan area of southern Zhejiang province. Celadon wares was made here from the Northern Song to the early Qing dynasty."}

{"id": "7b7a7f15-0e56-46e1-8ee0-c0b78cb20e33", "value": "Zimbabwe series beads reached southern Africa will not be possible until the source of the glass is found. Mid -13th to late 15th Centuries AD."}

{"id": "ac48aa5d-2041-4c3a-83ee-665ecc698219", "value": "Description: ndo-Pacific Beads are rarely more than 5mm in diameter and made in a limited range of colours including: opague reddish brown orange yellow green and black as well as semi-translucent greens and blues and translucent amber and violet. The glass often contains many bubbles and can vary in quality. The beads were so widely distributed both spatially and temporally. They were traded to West Africa with the Kingdom of Ghana by the 7th to 8th centuries Ad including at such sites as Tegdaoust in modern Mauritania Jenne-jenno in the Interior Niger Delta of Mali Beads may have arrived through internal African routes from East Africa. In Eastern Africa and Southern Africa Indo-Pacific glass beads are found at numerous sites dating from the early 7th to 8th centuries (AD) onwards. For example they have been recovered at sites such as Nzwanzi in the Comoros (11th - 15th centuries AD) post-Zhizo assemblages in southern Africa and multiple sites along the coast of East Africa (and particularly from Swahili Stonetowns). It is having also been suggested that some East Coast Indo-Pacific beads could have been manufactured between the 13th and 14th century at Mkokotoni on Zanzibar Island. | Description: mid-10th to mid-13th centuries AD. Type of glass from South and Southeast Asia. the K2 I-P series which is ubiquitous in southern Africa is not common in East Africa and those I have managed to identify tend to come from more southerly sites such as Kaole (see Paper VI) and Sanje ya Kati in southern Tanzania."}

{"id": "c5700ea9-92dd-4e08-a18b-16945c7a3e3f", "value": "early 9th century (AD) - Tang (T\u2019ang) Dynasty. Ceramic ware manufactured in Changsha kilns during the Tang dynasty varied greatly in form. They are unglazed brown-painted stoneware from the Tongguan kiln sites in Hunan Province."}

{"id": "ccca143f-03c1-412a-ac42-a574e31db38f", "value": "9th\u201311th centuries (AD) earthenware with probably origins in the Persian Gulf is termed lustre ware. This ware has soft to buff paste with a fine temper and fairly smooth fracture. The external surface is glazed with silvery-brown lustre giving it a shiny metallic appearance."}

{"id": "88e1765c-f6ac-4763-9e50-fa05bbbbdae2", "value": "The Middle East and in particular Egypt and the Levant played an important part in the history of glass where it it is generally acknowledged to have been invented in Mesopotamia in the middle of the third millennium BC. Middle East glass beads are commonly referred to as Phoenician beads and are spread around the Mediterranean littoral. Innovative glass beadmaking techniques where initiated in the Helenistic times and persisted trhought the Roman Empire into the Byzantine-Coptic periods and until the end of the Easly Islamd Period. The most widespread of glass beads from the Middle East are small monochrome oblate segmented beads recovered from Europe Middle East and Africa. These beads date from about 300 BCE to about 1200 CE and were an important staple in the Asian Maritime Trade network. | Produced from about 300 BCE to around 1200 CE Middle Eastern segmented glass beads have been identified in Europe the Middle East and Africa and are characteristically small monochrome oblates. They are however scarce in the Asian martime bead trade possibly due to competition with the numerous Indo-Pacific beads."}

{"id": "81faa41a-767d-44c3-809e-dd5e5cf5f57f", "value": "~500 BCE - present | Early Period (Phase 1) : 500 BC-100 AD Timbuktu\u2019s prehistoric phase (c . 500\u2013400 BC to c . AD 900\u20131000) The most common decorative technique in Period/Phase 1 is twine impression (see Figure 6.21). Over 50% of the sherds from this Phase are decorated with twine alone. About 9% of sherds from this phase have fine channeling along the lip of the rim. When Twine is present on the early sherds it is often incorporated onto the lip of the rim (see Figure 6.35) as well as the shoulder and body. Twine 6/7 is by far the most common technique in the Phase and indeed within all other phases at Tombouze. Later in Period/Phase 1 black paint is applied to the outer surface but this is a relatively uncommmon occurrence."}

{"id": "753a6787-a1b9-40d1-b0be-2422e3a0a286", "value": "Late Period (Phases 4 + 5) : AD 650-1000 Timbuktu\u2019s prehistoric phase (c . 500\u2013400 BC to c . AD 900\u20131000) The pottery assemblage from Phase 4 changes drastically from Phase 3. At TBZ1 where Phase 4 lies directly on top of Phase 3 the change occurs immediately after the end of Level 5. Simple open rims dominate the assemblage and about 78% of the assemblage is comprised of open vessels. This is a major change from Periods 1 and 2 where the most common type of vessel wad restricted. The most common type of rims is Rim H which makes up 44\u00b5 of the assembkages alone. These rims are long and everted. They often have deep and thick channeling (probably made by fingers as the rim is formed on a slow wheel). This vessel for is used for multiple activities (storage cooking and perhaps serving) and they come in all sizes. Rim H vessels (also known as 'long everted rim vessels) are all highly constricted at the neck are usually carinated at the widest part of the body and all have rounded bases (see Figures 6.43 and 6.44). Many were found within hearth and other domestic contexts. Others were found associated with grave contexts. Able to be used in multiple circumstances and contexts Rim H vessels semm to be the Swiss-army knife of vessel type found at Tombouze. It is in Phase 4 that obvious signs of cooking vecome common in the assembkage. About 28% of the vessels from Phase 4 show signs of cooking up from about 5% in either the Early and MIddle Periods. Also the ceramic paste becomes coarser the amount of the fine wares decreases to the lowest numbers observed at Tombouze. The decorative motifs are quite beautiful in Phase 4. Small restricted carinated pots (Rim I) often have triangularly-zoned and sequential bands decorated with the fine comb impressions just above the carination. Overall the quality of Phase 4 pots is quite impressive suggesting that a highly advanced style was brought into the region from somewhere else. However it is too early in our research efforts to suggest where the pottery may have come from"}

{"id": "1320b53a-ee0b-4515-9eec-bd55daa23cc1", "value": "Middle Period (Phases 2 + 3) : AD 100-650 Timbuktu\u2019s prehistoric phase (c . 500\u2013400 BC to c . AD 900\u20131000) Phase 2 (AD 100-430): Like Phase 1 before it the pottery assemblage from this phase is primarily comprised of closed vessels in the form of restricted globular jars. However the rim forms from Phase 2 are quite different than Phase 1. Phase 3 is much the same as Phase 2. The only difference is that Rim E1.1 is introduced to the assemblage for the first time and seems to be time sensitive to Phase 3. Also it is in Phase 3 that very large and open serving vessels appear."}

{"id": "07b4abcc-476e-436a-b452-b25247cc4d80", "value": "Recent Period (Phase 6/7): AD 1000-Present Phase 6/7 (AD 1000-Present): The most recent ceramic assemblages at Tombouze were not discovered during the excavations at either TBZ1 and TBZ2. However a number were recovered as surface finds during the intensive survey of the region. The Phase 6/7 ceramics (Phase 6 belonging to the time before the introduction of the tobacco pipe to West Africa in 1591) Phase 7 belonging to the time after 1591 which coincides with the general decline of historic Timbuktu are comprised of stamped and stabbed plastic designs. They do not have the fine fabric observed in the Early Period. They do not have the complex painted geometric designs of the Middle Period and none of the red slipped and burnished surface treatments of the Late Period. Moreover the rim styles are completely different and are often very constricted small and with heavily thickened rims."}

{"id": "608714ac-f377-4746-9952-de1105355b27", "value": "~500 BCE - present | Early Period (Phase 1) : 500 BC-100 AD Timbuktu\u2019s prehistoric phase (c . 500\u2013400 BC to c . AD 900\u20131000) The most common decorative technique in Period/Phase 1 is twine impression (see Figure 6.21). Over 50% of the sherds from this Phase are decorated with twine alone. About 9% of sherds from this phase have fine channeling along the lip of the rim. When Twine is present on the early sherds it is often incorporated onto the lip of the rim (see Figure 6.35) as well as the shoulder and body. Twine 6/7 is by far the most common technique in the Phase and indeed within all other phases at Tombouze. Later in Period/Phase 1 black paint is applied to the outer surface but this is a relatively uncommmon occurrence."}

{"id": "5014f7b6-7138-4266-8297-03762d615861", "value": "Kadzi ceramics are characteriscally thick-walled similar to other Early Farming Community Wares with out-turned lips and are often decorated on the lips and rims with comb-stamping technique. Ceramics have been recovered at sites in northern Zimbabwe in the mid-Zambezi valley region such as at Kadzi Kamukombe and Chigu. The sites are generally associated with higher faunal assemblages that have higher percentages of wild versus domesticates as well as evidence of finger millet (Eleusine coracana) and metal working and iron and copper artefacts."}

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: {"id": "545fe6aa-9d02-4cd6-bdff-7a2cd5b4ed43", "value": "The most striking marker of this period is the widespread use of bone to produce standardised artifact types known as points. LSA is also associated with the manufacture of art objects and ornaments especially beads and pendants made in bone and shell inclduing ostritch eggshell beads | The LSA in Ethiopia is characterised with the development of a microlithic industry. Many terminologies have been applied to this period including the Mode4/5 Industry Blade Mode 4 Industry as well as the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition which has been divided into three discrete temporal phases. Currently the earliest date for the start of the LSA in Ethiopia is 27 kya. Evidence indicates that microlithic tools were being manufactured well within the Aksumite Period in the form of highly standardised scrapers. Microlithic technologies also co-occur with the first evidence of pottery in northern Ethiopia dated to around 4700 years ago and with the presence of domestic livestock in the faunal remains. The industry also co-occurs with the presence of grindstones and later with classical and late Aksumite pottery dating from the fifth to sixth centuries AD. | Based on Brandt (1980) and Clark and Williams (1978) classification of the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition phase A refers to a transitional and emergent microlithic industry characterised by the use of local obsidian on backed geometric microliths and scrapers. Date range: 22 to 19 kya. The start date should be taken as tentative as the radiocarbon date from which it derives is made on ostrich eggshell. Note that this phase has been based on research conducted in and around Lake Besaka Rift Valley Ethiopia."}

{"id": "2aca4d05-7efd-4c71-a6c7-3125e2f6e9e1", "value": "Regosols are weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated medium and fine-textured material - more 
coarse-textured soils are Arenosols (in the case of sand) or Leptosols (in the case of gravel). Regosols 
show only slight signs of soil development - some accumulation of organic matter producing a somewhat 
darker topsoil is often the only evidence of soil formation. Limiting factors for soil development range 
from low temperatures, prolonged dryness, characteristics of the parent material or erosion. Regosols 
are extensive in eroding lands such as mountains or deserts where soil formation is generally absent."}

{"id": "e814a550-4a72-4875-ae6a-7c0399b47b92", "value": "A broader term for the Bronze Age period within Upper Nubia generally defined by the Kerma culture and its precursor the Pre-Kerma. The Kerma (although possibly not the Pre-Kerma) is also defined as part of a broader Kingdom of Kush the first polity referred to as such but due to the discontinuity between this Kingdom and the later Kingdom of Kush centred around Napata and Meroe they have been defined separately here. 3500BCE - 1450 BCE. | The Pre-Kerma is a cultural period in Upper Nubia preceding the Kerma civilisation and with many similar characteristics. It also has some similarities to the A-Group of Lower Nubia especially regarding pottery. | First period of Kerman culture. Territorial authority seemingly divided but with Kerma itself as leading power. May have been the period during which the great Deffufa was built at Kerma (Bonnet 2004). Also known as Kerma Ancien."}

{"id": "0071ae84-2bcd-4ed0-8ed8-6fbae7e6136b", "value": "Second period of Kerman culture. Kerma town is greatly expanded during this time reflecting its importance as a major centre. Also known as Kerma Moyen or very occasionally Old Kush II."}

{"id": "3bf75cf8-a23f-4876-a805-e1f3521b2a5c", "value": "The development of the pottery style continues in the Recent Pre-Kerma. The pottery is similiar to the Middle Pre-Kerma. It is polished has a black top und it is rippled limited to the rim. Additionally there is a geometric incised pattern. The artefacts show similiarities to sites between the second and the fourth cataracts."}

{"id": "4f3a32ad-ff78-43da-8824-1162311179d4", "value": "The most important archaeological sites at Gao itself are Gao-San\u00e9 (a tell north of the modern town) and Gao Ancien (beneath it) (Insoll 1997 2000). One or both probably formed the centre of the \u2018kingdom of Kawkaw\u2019 referred to by Al-Yaq\u016bb\u012b in 872/3. Unfortunately extensive looting at Gao-San\u00e9 has precluded its further dating beyond estimates obtained by the Malian Mission Inventaire of the 1980s (Raimbault and Sanogo 1991). Early occupation layers at Gao Ancien date to the middle centuries of the first millennium AD (Insoll 1998 2000) allowing ample time for the development of the substantial polity noted by Al-Yaq\u016bb\u012b. Date range: ~ 700CE - ~1200 CE | ~700 CE - ~900 CE"}

{"id": "58026c99-451b-491a-a665-a9c5e8ee78d7", "value": "In Senegal the megaliths are distributed along the Gambia River covering an area of about 38000 km\u00b2. The structures are constituted by frontal monoliths made of laterite which are located to the east of funerary monuments of various forms. They can be circles of standing stones stone circles or stone mounds. About 29000 standing stones make up a little less than 17000 monuments spread over nearly 2000 sites. It is generally accepted that they were built between the 7th and 15th centuries AD. | This phase is characterised by the strong presence of vases and it also sees the remergence of white paste vessels. Vases are typically cylindrical and decorated with twisted cord wheels. Pottery recovered from Wanar."}

{"id": "4a1c2228-c4c6-412f-8f2d-b28a27cac191", "value": "Woolandale is understood to be phase of Leopard\u2019s Kopje's pottery. It is characterised by graphite burnishing to redslipping just as at Khami."}

{"id": "618a419e-192d-4c59-a0b9-7bca1881e960", "value": "Musengenzi ceramics are found predominantly in northern Zimbabwean and are associated with multiple burials in rock shelters crevices or caves interred with a number of pots and bowls as well as other items of material culture. Musengezi ceramics are characterised by wrapped-fibre or bead-impressed decorations. Dated between 1100 to 1599 CE."}

{"id": "446799fc-0056-4037-ba7f-d49c800604ba", "value": "The earliest recorded facies of the Moloko branch in southern Africa is Icon which first appears in the Phalaborwa area and Limpopo Province of South Africa and perhaps Botswana dating to between about AD 1300 and 1500."}

{"id": "9adc71e3-1e5f-4c54-a2e0-9f4af376afe5", "value": "Between 1050 CE to around 1300 CE several chiefdoms developed and replaced the Zhizo/Taukome tradition. This includes Toutswe which covers southeastern Botswana from Palapye Shoshong to the Mmashoro and Mosu Area and Shoshong. Toutswe pottery is directly derived out of the Zhizo ceramic facies."}

{"id": "e52e606d-da10-494a-8e90-63a3112e02e1", "value": "Karanga is an architectural tradition characterised by defensible settlement patterns associated with Karanga-speakers of southern Zimbabwe who were set to repel the Ndebele and Gaza invasions during the 19th century."}

{"id": "ecb54c58-eeb7-4e1f-a0cb-ba4fceae4c2f", "value": "Letsibogo ceramic assemblages form part of the second phase of the early Moloko sequence. Letsibogo ceramics are characterised by arcades horizontal bands and lozenges bordered by dragged punctate lines or short grooves and filled in with red ochre and graphite colouring. Highly decorated bowls are also characteristic of these ceramic assemblages. Letsibogo ceramics occur predominantly in southeastern Botswana extending into the Limpopo Province of South Africa. Date range: 1500 - 1700 CE."}

{"id": "4cfbcdbc-f82e-4499-b606-770ba942fb19", "value": "Refers to a ceramic facies occuring between AD 1700 - 1850 relating to early Sotho/Tswana history and are often found in settlements with Molokwane type walling."}

{"id": "87157948-61ef-4223-98c6-4ede29fe2ffd", "value": "Named after the type site Khami located in southwestern Zimbabwe is a type of elite settlements characterised by terraced drystone walled capitals. The tradition is widely distributed in central and southwestern Zimbabwe eastern and southeastern Botswana and the adjacent area of northern South Africa. Other notable sites in Zimbabwe include Natletale and Danan'ombe and in Botswana these include Torahjuu Domboshava and Toutswemogala. Khami pottery is characterised by black and red designs on tall necks and shoulders of constricted vessels. Architecture: Terraced walls few freestanding enclosures Date: AD 1250\u2013AD 1900"}

{"id": "edfc8b90-528d-49fa-9476-f8cf2e1214fb", "value": "Description 1: Moloko is characterised by its ceramic tradition and have traditionally been divided into four main time segments. The first segment dating between 1300 CE and 1450 CE has been related to Icon and sites with this pottery occur predominantly in the Limpopo Province of South Africa and possibly in southeastern Botswana. During the second phase of the Moloko tradition there is a southwards expansion onto the Western Highveld in South Africa. Early Moloko sites are found in southeastern Botswana and in the northern parts of eastern South Africa dating from the 14th century CE. Sites tend to have a central cattle enclosure (kraal) with surrounding houses. Towards the end of the second phase and during the third phase (1500 - 1700 CE) low-stone walling appears with shifts in settlement organisation. The fourth phase of the Moloko ceramic sequence is suggested to be ancestral to Sotho and Tswana speaking communities dating back to the 18th and 19th centuries. Three ceramic types are seen to have developed from the Moloko second phase: Letsibogo (eastern Botswana) Madikwe (southeastern Botswana and the North-West Province of South Africa) and Olifantspoort (Magaliesberg South Africa). Early ceramic assemblages (before 1700 CE) have a relatively high stylistic variability with a large number of decorated bowl classes. Description 2: Moloko includes at least three separate facies derived from Icon each with a similar direction of change in motifs: Letsibogo in Botswana Madikwe in North West Province (South Africa) and Botswana and Olifantspoort in the Magaliesberg area (South Africa). Emphases on different decoration techniques separate these three facies. Otherwise the range of stylistic types is remarkably similar. Radiocarbon dates place this second phase between about AD 1500 and 1700. In all three areas the second phase predates stonewalling ascribed to Tswana speakers (see Huffman 2020)."}

{"id": "8307b2ba-57f4-44e1-b8a1-ca61469f59ea", "value": "Definition 1: Ceramics are named after the type site of Leopard's Kopje near Khami a World Heritage Site in Zimbabwe. The ceramics are widely distributed from west-central Zimbabwe to north-eastern Botswana as well as adjacent areas of northern South Africa. Leopard\u2019s Kopje occurs at sites from around AD 1000 such as at Mapela Mapungubwe Woolandale and Khami among other places. It is suggested that the makers of Leopard's Kopje ceramics were ancestors ot western Shona-speakers. It is characterised by single and multiple lines or bands of comb- or dentate-stamping on the necks and shoulders of jars. including incised arcades and triangles on the neck and lower neck/shoulder areas of jars. Description: ...show clustering of sizeable settlements that can be called towns and judging from the number of pens and depth of cow dung present at them also housed sizeable cattle herds. This process of urbanization provided competition for resources among later Zhizo type settlements in eastern Botswana as Leopard's Kopje sites in the middle Limpopo Valley seem to have had better access to foreign goods whose transhipment into the interior they controlled by virtue of their position along the river and relative proximity to the coast (Manyanga et al 2010)."}

{"id": "aaed09ca-4ab7-444e-ac61-1fa72e21c40a", "value": "Mambo is a northern cluster of ceramics of the Leopard's Kopje ceramic assemblage distributed in southwestern Zimbabwe and northeastern Botswana."}

{"id": "7396e624-09ff-4124-9afb-8242d8d8efbc", "value": "Ceramic Definition: The K2 ceramics are widely distributed in western and central Zimbabwe and northeastern Botswana and the adjacent areas of northern South Africa. The key features of K2 ceramics include hatched bands on the neck and beaker bottoms as well as upright incised triangles on the neck. Description: One of the largest settlements Bambandyanalo grew in size (to over 8 ha) and shows social and economic specialization as attested by evidence for ivory working. However while informative as to the lifestyle demography and health of the site's inhabitants (Meyer 1998) the quite extensive available skeletal sample does not provide much evidence for social strati cation although ethnographic data suggest that some of the people buried in the cattle pen were probably of high status. Social strati cation however becomes clear at nearby (1km distant) Mapungubwe Hill which was inhabited from c. 1220 to 1300."}

{"id": "c67ac1a1-1eeb-4330-a352-c9696db2a479", "value": "The period is marked by the beginning of the southern Africa's incorporation into the expanding economic system including agropastoral craft production and commercial connections with the Indian Ocean and Central Africa leading to greater socio-political complexity and the emergence of early urbanism and statehood. Late Farming Communities in southern Africa begins approximately 1000 CE and continues into the historic period. Linguistic evidence suggests that ancestors of present-day language or dialect groups in southern Africa date from the early second millennium AD. Examples include the Shona of the Zimbabwe plateau and adjacent lowlands in Mozambique and the Sotho/Tswana and Nguni south of the Limpopo River. Use more specific type where known. | Refers to a ceramic facies occuring between AD 1700 - 1850 relating to early Sotho/Tswana history and are often found in settlements with Molokwane type walling."}

{"id": "f78345ea-8ecc-4ada-aa35-404095ab330d", "value": "Olifantspoort ceramic assemblages form part of the second phase of the early Moloko sequence and occurs in the Magaliesberg area of South Africa. The ceramic assemblage is characterised with fine hatching. Date range: 1500 - 1700 CE."}

{"id": "2ca6f0fd-97c8-480c-a0db-ae7d7e5becde", "value": "Gumanye pottery occurs over much of south-central Zimbabwe and adjacent regions of northern South Africa. Ceramics are plain with occassional incisons. In Zimbabwe it has been recovered from sites such as Gumanye Hill in Chivi District Chivowa Hill and on the hill at Great Zimbabwe. It is mostly found overlain by Zimbabwe pottery and suggested to be ancestral to Great Zimbabwe periods III and IV."}

{"id": "5f5a0d6d-8b8e-4842-8a2a-c41fa5bf4294", "value": "The spread of a new culture can be traced by the distribution of Mapungubwe pottery. This style developed between AD 1220 and AD 1250. The pottery is named after the capital of Mapungubwe situated in the Shashe-Limpopo River Basin. This site is identified as a rainmaking hill with sacred leadership and a dual settlement system indicating a class-based society. The site of Mapungubwe is believed to have been abandoned from around AD 1300 relating to climatic change and marking the beginning of the 'Little Ice Age'. Description of Mapungubwe site: . The inhabitants of this town who probably numbered more than 5000 traded in copper iron ivory glass beads and gold which is the reason why their rulers were so wealthy. The burial evidence from the hilltop shows considerable social stratification"}

{"id": "ba6a5826-1b54-4693-8179-f1c7912b1f81", "value": "The Nyanga Complex (architectural) represents an agricultural society of industrious farmers and stock-raisers. Sites are mostly characterised by stone-faced terraces covering hills and valleys as well as stone-built homesteads and defensive forts or refuges extending from Ruangwe in the north of Nyanga District to the Pungwe Valley in the south to Cumberland Valley Burnaby in the south west and into Tanda/Chinyika west of the Nyangombe river of Zimbabwe. This covers an area of some 5000 square kilometres. Areas with lesser outlying occurrences are in the Makha area of Mutoko west of Headlands/Weya and south of Chimanimani. The walled villages with linteled entrances in the area northeast of Rusape including at Diana's Vow site and at the site Harleigh Farm are thought to be related to the Nyanga Complex. Ann Kritzinger argues that mining activity not agriculture explains the archaeology of the Nyanga terraces in the Eastern Highlands (see for example Kritzinger A. 2009. Early Mining and Metallurgy in Zimbabwe\u201f s Eastern Highlands. Mining History 17(4) pp.79-82 Kritzinger A. 2008. Gold not grain: precolonial harvest in the terraced hills of Zimbabwe's Eastern highlands. Cookeia (13) pp.1-42. Kritzinger A. 2012. Laboratory analysis reveals direct evidence of precolonial gold recovery in the archaeology of Zimbabwe\u2019s Eastern Highlands. Proceedings of 9th International Mining History Kritzinger A. 2010. Gradient and soil analysis identify the function of stone-built tunnels in the archaeology of the Eastern Highlands Zimbabwe. Nyame Akuma 73 pp.10-16."}

{"id": "f98c2e52-2455-439b-8848-df2670285eb8", "value": "Madikwe ceramics form part of the second phase of the early Moloko sequence and ancestral to present-day Sotho and Tswana speaking communities. Madikwe occurs predominantly in southeastern Botswana and the North-West Province of South Africa. The pottery is highly decorated. Date range: 1500 - 1700 CE."}
{"id": "0ae81b66-db1f-4d4c-b620-d1613d9a9c10", "value": "Harare pottery represents LFC settlements in northern Zimbabwe dated between the 10th and 15th century."}

{"id": "7e63aebd-3928-4f78-9349-adbc2e7af411", "value": "During the 15th Century Great Zimbabwe lost some of its influence in the northern and western parts of the Zimbabwe Plateau with the appearance of other centres constucted along similar lines to Great Zimbabwe. One of which was the formation of the Mutapa State beginning around c.1450 in northern Zimbabwe. The rise of the Mutapa State is captured extensively in Portuguese written sources where early Portuguese explorers in the interior reported stone buildings. Archaeological evidence also indicates the presence of imported artefacts through trade with eastern Africa as well as locally manufactured pottery that have been related to the ethnic group of the Karanga. This has also been attested to by Portuguese records. By the 16th Century African-Portuguese trading posts and settlements are found and associated with locally manufactured pottery as well as traded items including imported ceramics and glass. It is also at the beginning of the 16th Century where stone-building ceases with the emergence of non-stone-walled royal courts. The decline of the Mutapa State has been suggested to be triggered by the exploitative nature of the Portuguese merchants and conquistadores in northern Zimbabwe in connection with goldmining and the subsequent building of fortifications by the late 16th and early 17th century. The crudely built stone defenses or wooden stockades were often erected on hilltops.Ceramic evidence from these hillforts suggest that the Budya or related Tonga groups from the lower Zambezi as the builders."}

{"id": "0a8272dc-4499-42bd-80ac-e123f03543e5", "value": "Mahonje is an architectural and ceramic tradition found predominantly in north-eastern Zimbabwe and linked to numerous hillltop settlements with roughly circular coarse stone enclosures. The enclosures are characteristically equipped with loopholes whose function is not yet clear. Items of Mahonje material culture include imported beads and ceramics."}

{"id": "c7ea1dc4-a50b-437a-999b-4a5a6cec92ed", "value": "The Lower Palaeolithic extends from 300000 to 75000 BC. The sites of Kar\u00e9 and Sansand\u00e9 (eastern Senegal) represent the most characteristic archaeological stations of its Acheulean culture. Indeed the tools are characterized by scrapers and tools on pebbles cut in microchoppers and micochopping-tools. Bifaces and axes are also tools that refer to this culture but are rare. | The Acheulean is a facies of the Lower Paleolithic and is characterized by the culture of bifaces and axes."}

{"id": "e54e554e-a64d-4c98-8f25-bde0e71c4ef7", "value": "Often confused with Goulets, Keyhole monuments have an inner and outer enclosure giving them the appearance of a cairn surrounded by two concentric circles or ellipses. May include a number of intrusive tumuli and/or other later structures, sometimes the stone taken from the keyhole itself. Keyhole monuments exhibit greater relief than goulets, with raised enclosure perimeters. In a keyhole monument, the outer perimeter tends to be complete, closing the end of the corridor. Keyhole monuments exhibit less pronounced asymmetry, and may be wider at the end housing the tumulus."}

{"id": "31738b35-ea89-4b13-a787-0c6ec6321979", "value": "Le terme \"shell midden\" d\u00e9signe un tel amas compos\u00e9 principalement de coquilles de MOLLUSCS et/ou d'autres animaux \u00e0 coquille tels que les ECHINODERMES et les ARTHROPODS. Le terme \"shell midden\" \u00e9tait autrefois couramment utilis\u00e9 pour d\u00e9signer un type de site arch\u00e9ologique, mais il est maintenant surtout employ\u00e9 pour d\u00e9signer un type de caract\u00e9ristique arch\u00e9ologique.Ainsi, les d\u00e9p\u00f4ts de coquillages sont des caract\u00e9ristiques que l'on retrouve dans certains sites arch\u00e9ologiques, avec d'autres types de d\u00e9p\u00f4ts, tels que des couches de sol naturel, des sols modifi\u00e9s par l'homme, des sols d'habitation, des foyers, des fosses de stockage, des caract\u00e9ristiques mortuaires, etc. https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/shell-middens"}

{"id": "d7c35b75-c374-4db2-83cd-c1e347028599", "value": "Shell midden refers to such a heap composed predominantly of the shells of MOLLUSCS and/or other shell-bearing animals such as ECHINODERMS and ARTHROPODS. The term shell midden was once commonly used to designate an archaeological site type but is now mostly employed to refer to a type of archaeological feature. Thus, shell middens are features that occur in some bearing archaeological sites, along with other types of deposits, such as natural soil layers, anthropogenically modified soils, dwelling floors, hearths, storage pits, mortuary features and so on. https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/shell-middens"}

{"id": "8b600e2e-a369-40ad-a600-f07e32704e3d", "value": "La technique de l'enduit est une m\u00e9thode de construction composite utilis\u00e9e pour la construction de murs et de b\u00e2timents, dans laquelle un treillis tiss\u00e9 de bandes de bois appel\u00e9 enduit est enduit d'un mat\u00e9riau collant g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement compos\u00e9 d'une combinaison de terre humide, d'argile, de sable, de fumier et de paille."}

{"id": "3104a73c-40a3-40d6-9445-4fc2f00aaa65", "value": "Wattle and daub is a composite building method used for making walls and buildings, in which a woven lattice of wooden strips called wattle is daubed with a sticky material usually made of some combination of wet soil, clay, sand, animal dung and straw."}
