{"id": "177c247b-2b6b-42ca-84d6-67e94b584146", "value": "This property associates an instance of E18 Physical Thing with another instance of Physical Thing that forms part of it. The spatial extent of the composing part is included in the spatial extent of the whole. Component elements, since they are themselves instances of E18 Physical Thing, may be further analysed into sub-components, thereby creating a hierarchy of part decomposition. An instance of E18 Physical Thing may be shared between multiple wholes, for example two buildings may share a common wall. This property does not specify when and for how long a component element resided in the respective whole. If a component is not part of a whole from the beginning of existence or until the end of existence of the whole, the classes E79 Part Addition and E80 Part Removal can be used to document when a component became part of a particular whole and/or when it stopped being a part of it. For the time-span of being part of the respective whole, the component is completely contained in the place the whole occupies. This property is intended to describe specific components that are individually documented, rather than general aspects. Overall descriptions of the structure of an instance of E18 Physical Thing are captured by the P3 has note property. The instances of E57 Material of which an instance of E18 Physical Thing is composed should be documented using P45 consists of (is incorporated in). This property is transitive and asymmetric."}

{"id": "1c400ec7-b46a-40f6-94c5-74696d378942", "value": "Grassy woodlands are communities that have trees in the overstorey that are widely spaced, not overlapping; shrub cover is sparse. The predominant vegetation is grasses; herbs or forbs may be highly diverse."}

{"id": "1eaacf86-38ee-40af-bc4d-36e0d0d6a8f7", "value": "Les for\u00eats de gramin\u00e9es sont des communaut\u00e9s dont les arbres de l'\u00e9tage dominant sont tr\u00e8s espac\u00e9s et ne se chevauchent pas ; la couverture arbustive est rare. La v\u00e9g\u00e9tation pr\u00e9dominante est constitu\u00e9e de gramin\u00e9es ; les herbes et les plantes herbac\u00e9es peuvent \u00eatre tr\u00e8s diversifi\u00e9es."}

{"id": "ab32e3dd-9498-429a-aa84-0617c604736e", "value": "This category includes all developed land, including transportation infrastructure and human settlements of any size, unless they are already included under other categories. {"id": "fa2f0c81-d6c6-48bc-956e-517e54fc5b7e", "value": "Cette cat\u00e9gorie comprend toutes les terres am\u00e9nag\u00e9es, y compris les infrastructures de transport et les \u00e9tablissements humains de toute taille, \u00e0 moins qu'ils ne soient d\u00e9j\u00e0 inclus dans d'autres cat\u00e9gories. Cela devrait \u00eatre coh\u00e9rent avec la s\u00e9lection des d\u00e9finitions nationales."}

{"id": "1f86cc45-8a88-4255-907b-c5bfb55b8b85", "value": "Le bush est un peuplement ouvert de buissons (g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement entre 3 et 7 m de haut) avec une couverture de 40 % ou plus. Le fourr\u00e9 est un peuplement ferm\u00e9 de buissons et de plantes grimpantes mesurant g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement entre 3 et 7 m de haut."}

{"id": "3938eab4-c2c5-47ae-8667-752b9223b0fa", "value": "Bushland is an open stand of bushes (usually between 3 and 7 m tall) with a canopy cover of 40 percent or more. Thicket is a closed stand of bushes and climbers usually between 3 and 7 m tall."}

{"id": "087c8fe6-073c-47ba-9080-ceb6ded1e21a", "value": "Zones caract\u00e9ris\u00e9es par une v\u00e9g\u00e9tation herbac\u00e9e naturelle ou semi-naturelle ; la v\u00e9g\u00e9tation herbac\u00e9e repr\u00e9sente 75 % \u00e0 100 % de la couverture."}
{"id": "0b6061eb-325e-4cf6-8687-df825d1cee9d", "value": "Areas characterized by natural or semi-natural herbaceous vegetation; herbaceous vegetation accounts for 75% to 100% of the cover."}

{"id": "f4883f59-5603-41da-be7d-d691060f9535", "value": "Zones de substratum rocheux, de pavement d\u00e9sertique, d'escarpements, d'\u00e9boulis, de glissements, de mat\u00e9riaux volcaniques, de d\u00e9bris glaciaires, de dunes de sable, de mines \u00e0 ciel ouvert, de gravi\u00e8res et d'autres accumulations de mat\u00e9riaux terreux. En g\u00e9n\u00e9ral, la v\u00e9g\u00e9tation repr\u00e9sente moins de 15 % de la couverture totale."}

{"id": "4028f1ff-7895-4824-8baa-a3f2012f3436", "value": "Areas of bedrock, desert pavement, scarps, talus, slides, volcanic material, glacial debris, sand dunes, strip mines, gravel pits, and other accumulations of earthen material. Generally, vegetation accounts for less than 15% of total cover."}
{"id": "fce6f28a-65f2-4ce8-b482-45cb29e7d19a", "value": "a closed stand of bushes and climbers usually between 3 and 7 m tall"}

{"id": "c3c3fa12-6a61-4819-8731-2d62173d8604", "value": "A transitional vegetation formation of local extent that is intermediate between woodland and bushland (an alternative definition is stunted woodland less than 8 m tall)"}

{"id": "d33d072c-8bc7-4887-a0ec-b0f00089d394", "value": "Formation v\u00e9g\u00e9tale transitoire d'\u00e9tendue locale interm\u00e9diaire entre la for\u00eat et le bushland (une autre d\u00e9finition est la for\u00eat rabougrie de moins de 8 m de haut)."}

{"id": "88a9fb6a-0d10-4980-90ca-53a3f980e651", "value": "Zones o\u00f9 le sol ou le substrat est p\u00e9riodiquement satur\u00e9 d'eau ou recouvert d'eau, selon la d\u00e9finition de Cowardin et al. (1979)."}
{"id": "fb90cde6-78af-455c-84e1-e17eef3f79f3", "value": "Areas where the soil or substrate is periodically saturated with or covered by water as defined by Cowardin et al. (1979)."}

{"id": "b1683969-6a99-4a55-8ccf-71c9281c6980", "value": "Les savanes bois\u00e9es sont des biomes qui couvrent 20 % de la surface terrestre mondiale et sont fortement concentr\u00e9es entre les for\u00eats pluviales \u00e9quatoriales et les d\u00e9serts et semi-d\u00e9serts des latitudes moyennes."}

{"id": "4ac51c31-a2f3-458d-bb1d-041395eeb09e", "value": "Woodlands savannas are biomes that cover 20% of the world's land surface and are highly concentrated between the equatorial rain forests and the mid-latitude deserts and semi-deserts."}

{"id": "7356e2aa-7670-4732-be1b-1ce8dbebee6d", "value": "La savane arbor\u00e9e est une v\u00e9g\u00e9tation caract\u00e9ris\u00e9e par une couverture v\u00e9g\u00e9tale compos\u00e9e de grandes herbes grossi\u00e8res de 2 \u00e0 3 m\u00e8tres de haut, parmi lesquelles se dressent de petits arbres noueux, g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement si \u00e9loign\u00e9s les uns des autres que le soleil n'a que peu ou pas de difficult\u00e9 \u00e0 p\u00e9n\u00e9trer jusqu'au sol ou au moins jusqu'\u00e0 la couche herbac\u00e9e."}

{"id": "5346c44f-a44f-4c1e-b32a-6a6f8fd9533c", "value": "Savannah woodlands is vegetation characterised by its ground cover of coarse, tall grasses 2-3 metres high, among which small gnarled trees stand, usually so far apart that the sun has little or no difficulty in penetrating to the ground or at least to the herbaceous layer."}

{"id": "437587ed-15f9-4133-a655-d446776ce2e5", "value": "Areas characterized by herbaceous vegetation that has been planted or is intensively managed to produce food, feed, or fiber, or is maintained in developed settings for specific purposes. Herbaceous vegetation accounts for 75% to 100% of the cover."}

{"id": "331df55c-0acd-48a9-9ac1-b2e5201488c9", "value": "Zones caract\u00e9ris\u00e9es par une v\u00e9g\u00e9tation herbac\u00e9e qui a \u00e9t\u00e9 plant\u00e9e ou qui est g\u00e9r\u00e9e de mani\u00e8re intensive pour produire des denr\u00e9es alimentaires, des aliments pour animaux ou des fibres, ou qui est maintenue dans des environnements am\u00e9nag\u00e9s \u00e0 des fins sp\u00e9cifiques. La v\u00e9g\u00e9tation herbac\u00e9e repr\u00e9sente 75 \u00e0 100 % de la couverture."}

{"id": "01c9f6ab-b535-498f-a4e1-ff1e0e7d9f45", "value": "Riverine forest is an area where the land and river interface. These forest areas are hotspots of aquatic and terrestrial biodiversity, with a wide range of floral structures (trees, shrubs, and grasses) and fauna (mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles)"}

{"id": "285ab612-05d8-47ed-aa4e-178d0807bb70", "value": "La for\u00eat riveraine est une zone d'interface entre la terre et la rivi\u00e8re. Ces zones foresti\u00e8res sont des hauts lieux de la biodiversit\u00e9 aquatique et terrestre, avec un large \u00e9ventail de structures florales (arbres, arbustes et herbes) et de faune (mammif\u00e8res, oiseaux, amphibiens et reptiles)."}

{"id": "94f29ff5-a01a-4bdc-94d4-c1e96685b5dd", "value": "Areas characterized by tree cover (natural or semi-natural woody vegetation, generally more than 6 meters tall); tree canopy accounts for 25% to 100% of the cover."}

{"id": "8d02b7a3-4059-4395-a48d-c4fe047fa2ee", "value": "Zones caract\u00e9ris\u00e9es par un couvert arbor\u00e9 (v\u00e9g\u00e9tation ligneuse naturelle ou semi-naturelle, g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement de plus de 6 m\u00e8tres de haut) ; le couvert arbor\u00e9 repr\u00e9sente de 25 % \u00e0 100 % de la couverture."}

{"id": "e1e6948d-6c25-4a1c-a1c1-988b5601cf71", "value": "Areas characterized by natural or semi-natural woody vegetation with aerial stems, generally less than 6 meters tall, with individuals or clumps not touching to interlocking. Both evergreen and deciduous species of true shrubs, young trees, and trees or shrubs that are small or stunted because of environmental conditions are included."}

{"id": "be7fbdaa-fc79-4f2d-b126-ee6956726c98", "value": "Zones caract\u00e9ris\u00e9es par une v\u00e9g\u00e9tation ligneuse naturelle ou semi-naturelle \u00e0 tiges a\u00e9riennes, g\u00e9n\u00e9ralement d'une hauteur inf\u00e9rieure \u00e0 6 m\u00e8tres, dont les individus ou les touffes ne se touchent pas et ne s'imbriquent pas les uns dans les autres. Les esp\u00e8ces \u00e0 feuilles persistantes et \u00e0 feuilles caduques de v\u00e9ritables arbustes, les jeunes arbres et les arbres ou arbustes de petite taille ou rabougris en raison des conditions environnementales sont inclus.\n\nTraduit avec www.DeepL.com/Translator (version gratuite)"}

{"id": "b652cbaa-2f40-474f-a71a-f5803b07ddbf", "value": "An edaphic formation of distinct physiognomy of open or closed stands of trees (or bushes) occurring on shores between the high- and low-water marks"}

{"id": "897d3ecb-5ab2-4d79-aa33-31dc38928b41", "value": "Formation \u00e9daphique de physionomie distincte de peuplements ouverts ou ferm\u00e9s d'arbres (ou de buissons) se trouvant sur les rivages entre la laisse de haute mer et la laisse de basse mer."}

{"id": "8e727f70-b60f-41dc-a7df-b737983560cd", "value": "Riparian vegetation corresponds to all vegetation units along river networks, regardless of their physiognomy or origin, and is functionally related to other components of fluvial systems and the surrounding area"}

{"id": "d0bea61f-4477-481f-a930-74e1aa156036", "value": "La v\u00e9g\u00e9tation riveraine correspond \u00e0 toutes les unit\u00e9s de v\u00e9g\u00e9tation le long des r\u00e9seaux fluviaux, ind\u00e9pendamment de leur physionomie ou de leur origine, et est fonctionnellement li\u00e9e \u00e0 d'autres composantes des syst\u00e8mes fluviaux et de la zone environnante."}

{"id": "cc60adae-32ca-410d-87b3-194ad488392f", "value": "Zones permanentes ou saisonni\u00e8res o\u00f9 la couverture v\u00e9g\u00e9tale est tr\u00e8s faible du fait de l'action de l'homme, c'est-\u00e0-dire de la disparition de la couverture d'arbres, de buissons et/ou d'herbac\u00e9es par rapport \u00e0 la couverture v\u00e9g\u00e9tale naturelle environnante. Cette cat\u00e9gorie comprend les principales cicatrices d'\u00e9rosion, c'est-\u00e0-dire l'\u00e9rosion en nappe et l'\u00e9rosion par ravinement."}

{"id": "71eb2ac6-339f-41a7-b033-c3e2f6c13da5", "value": "A kingdom in southern Central Sudan, centering on Soba near the Nile confluence. Southernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Also known in Arabic as \u2018Alwa\u2019. "}

{"id": "025b3297-9160-485c-943b-9ce40a3b7522", "value": "A temporally significant class of artifacts defined by a consistent clustering of attributes. The concept and related subcategories can be used where the chronology resource entry has been characterised by the presence and timing of a particular material cultural assemblage. Sub-categories of the material culture class include for example: Ceramics, Architectural style, Metallurgy, Wall painting, Furniture, Beads, Botanical, Fauna, Lithics, Textiles."}

{"id": "61bf7848-03c6-4b43-927b-7525fc74075f", "value": "Characterised by Incised Wavy Line pottery and distinctive Lunula type pottery decoration. The Dotted Wavy Line decoration rare but present. Post-holes suggest very light dwellings pointing to a mobile seasonal presence at some sites."}

{"id": "8585ec14-7da6-4e1f-8ffe-f79383236c74", "value": "The Middle Paleolithic is dated between 75 000 and 27 000 BC. It is distributed over a large part of Senegal (the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 the Niokolo-Koba Park the Senegal River valley the Cape Verde Peninsula). Characterised by side-scrapers notches backed knives Levallois and Moustero\u00efd Facies. | In Senegal the Mousteroid is not very characteristic of the Mousterian of Europe. It is generally defined by a tooling on flakes (points scrapers denticulates notches back knives rarity of burins and absence of typical scrapers) with small bifaces. The Mousteroid is very visible in the Cape Verde Peninsula where a series of surface deposits have been identified: Bargny Diokoul Cap des biches Ravin de Mbeth S\u00e9bikotane etc."}

{"id": "36a5b48e-2d13-4017-8ab0-5e937ac70cc1", "value": "A kingdom centred on Old Dongola in the Dongola Reach in Upper Nubia, which became dominant over the rest of Nubia from around the 7th to 14th centuries AD. Located in the middle of the \u2018Nubian\u2019 kingdoms."}

{"id": "cedd9a33-1a4a-41cd-939a-2c14e031bc06", "value": "A period in which the Middle Nile was ruled by 2-3 major kingdoms all of which had converted to Christianity by the late 6th century AD. While the term Medieval draws arguably problematic parallels to Europe and the Middle East and the term Christian is somewhat reductive and ignores the part of this period where these kingdoms were not primarily Christian the two are the only major terms used to refer to this period."}

{"id": "457e559b-30bc-45f2-9b09-ebe15bafa9c9", "value": "A period in which the Middle Nile was ruled by 2-3 major kingdoms all of which had converted to Christianity by the late 6th century AD. While the term Medieval draws arguably problematic parallels to Europe and the Middle East and the term Christian is somewhat reductive and ignores the part of this period where these kingdoms were not primarily Christian the two are the only major terms used to refer to this period. | A kingdom in Lower Nubia established around the 3rd century AD. Northernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Later it was conquered by Makuria in the 7th century AD."}

Northernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Later it was conquered by Makuria in the 7th century AD."}

{"id": "a9a073c6-0a49-4e79-a60e-f02b59d857e8", "value": "The abbreviation for \u201cBefore Present,\u201d used especially in radiocarbon dating. The fixed reference date for \u201cBefore Present\u201d has been established as 1950 AD. Thus, 4250 BP would mean 4250 years prior to 1950, or 2300 BC. The year 1950 was the latest that the atmosphere was sufficiently uncontaminated to act as a standard for radiocarbon dating. The lower case \u2018bp\u2019 represents uncalibrated radiocarbon years; the capitals BP denote a calibrated radiocarbon date, or a date derived from some other dating method, such as potassium-argon, that does not need calibration."}

{"id": "88c40b0e-9f9f-47b1-9a46-a66a00dfc608", "value": "The Mesolithic is a term used in Europe and sometimes western Asia and northern Africa to describe a variation in hunter-gatherer lifeways and possibly some precursors to agriculture occuring between the end of the Stone Age/Palaeolithic and the Neolithic. In Sudan this term is generally used interchangeably with the Epipalaeolithic a term normally applied to western Asia so within this database the terms are listed as synonyms. Although both terms originate outside of the region and so are in many ways problematic they are both used to describe sites and so must be included here. 9000BCE - 5000BCE. Although both Mesolithic and Epipalaeolithic originate outside of the region and so are in many ways problematic they are both used to describe sites and so must be included here | A lithic industry characterised by many single-platform cores. It is contemporary to the Epipalaeolithic in West Asia."}
{"id": "2d8fe159-2d16-479e-91ac-38417efb6312", "value": "Used for phases and/or events dating to the 27th century Before Common Era BCE/BC (2601 - 2700 BC/BCE)"}

{"id": "d701e125-a98e-477b-b31e-19db207801dc", "value": "The earliest type of pottery connected with farming communities in southern Africa. Ceramic assemblages occur in the southeastern part of southern Africa with early dates deriving from southern Mozambique Eswatini Zimbabwe and South Africa. The sites are associated with arable soils and iron ore deposits and the ceramics have high proportions of fluted rims on bowls and bevelled rims on jars. Mzonjani in South Africa is a later expression of Silver Leaves and widely occurs in the interior dating to around 550-650 CE. Several sites in eastern Botswana including Baratani ceramics appear to have a related expression of Mzonjani-dervied ceramic traditions."}

{"id": "62305129-d1ce-42ed-bb38-6a6a3b311141", "value": "Geospatial data on sites location and characteristics that have been identified throughfield survey and have been recorded using a tablet or other electronic device"}
{"id": "41b625a9-f8c1-401a-a6fa-e329ffb0309f", "value": "A written work issued at regular intervals, numbered consecutively with no intended or planned end point."}

{"id": "d5b71299-f3a7-457f-bb2a-13293f8e3af7", "value": "Defintion 1: Contentious chronological term referring to a type of pottery characterised by the use of several different wavy line decorations found both in the Nile Valley and across the wider Sahel-Sahara belt. Assumed to be a precursor to the Dotted Wavy Line by early researchers (e.g. Arkell) associated with the Khartoum Mesolithic vs Khartoum Neolithic but proven to be found in Khartoum Mesolithic/Neolithic occupations from beginning to end and found later than the Dotted Wavy Line in Sahara-Sahel contexts. Chronological associations have yet to be fully deciphered but current estimates suggest 10000BP - 4000BCE. Definition 2: Wavy Line is an incised decoration of pottery which appeared in the Mesolithic/Epipaleolithic of Sudan. It is connected to the Early Mesolithic."}

{"id": "97adb5e0-6ea6-464a-9ea9-5eded1a3940a", "value": "The investigator has limited reason (e.g. proximity to archaeology, nature/source of threat etc.,) to suggest that the threat is likely to cause future disturbance to the site (within 3-5 years). For example, the threat is relatively distant from the archaeology or appears to be related to a one-off, rather than ongoing, event."}

{"id": "a7fb20ef-2084-47e2-ac72-72e5bafd3f2b", "value": "The second epoch of the Quaternary and the most recent geologic interval of time. The name which means \u2018entirely recent' extends from about 11 700 BCE to the present. It coincides with the late and post-Stone Age history of the human species . It is also associated with the current interglacial (~11 700 BP - present day). Holocene stratigraphic records provide evidence inter alia of climate and sea-level change geomorphological and hydrological processes vegetational developments and faunal migrations. In addition they contain a unique range and wealth of archaeological data that attest to the development of society and the evolving relationships between people and the environment under near modern boundary conditions. | An informal tripartite subdivision of the Holocene that has long been employed and describes the earliest of three formally defined chronostratigraphic and geochronological units: the Lower/Early Middle and Upper/Late Holocene subseries/subepochs. This first stage/age of the Holocene is also termed the Greenlandian Stage/Age with its GSSP in the Greenland NGRIP2 ice core and dated at 11700 yr b2k (before 2000 CE) and is defined with its corrresponding Early Holocene Subseries/Subepoch.This subdivision was formally ratified by the Executive Committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) on 14th June 2018. | A stadial of the Weichselian cold stage dated to between 11000 and 10000BP. The last glacial recession (13000\u20136000 years ago) was interrupted by this sharp advance. It takes its name from a tundra plant called Dryas octopetala."}

{"id": "24388f2e-5de3-4e0e-82b3-363e0d6b6d5b", "value": "Definition 1: Late Pre-Aksumite Ceramics are haracterized by red\u2013orange bowls and red-brick jars with a cylindrical neck. Definition 2: The Late Pre- Aksumite phase (c. 400/300 BC) characterized by red\u2013orange bowls and red-brick jars with a cylindrical neck."}

{"id": "73d5ea38-2c65-4a30-919f-56f0c0327715", "value": "After the disintegration of Makuria the North of Sudan was ruled by various separate small feudal principalities which over time mostly converted from Christianity to Islam. These principalities continued to exist until the Ottoman conquest in 1820 and their rulers were often called Danaqla after the important city of Dongola. Similar events also occurred in the South although beginning slightly later after the disintegration of Alodia/Alwa and ending earlier with their coalescence under the 'Abdallab and then the Funj Sultanate. 1300CE - 1820C | The various Arab tribal federations in post-Alodia central and southern Sudan were united by 'Abdallah Jamma in the late 15th century CE before soon after being conquered by the Funj people from further south in the 16th century CE. 1475CE - 1504CE"}

{"id": "74f095d9-199a-4210-a425-682aa246a577", "value": "A technocomplex of the Terminal Pleistocene/Early Holocene Later Stone Age industry characterised with a non-microlithic assemblage. Formal tools are few except for large scrapers though scrapers with adze-like lateral retouch are common after ca. 7500 BCE. The technocomplex dates between 12000 and 7000 years ago BP. Regional variants include Albany (southern and eastern Cape Fold Belt South Africa) Kuruman (Northern Cape South Africa) Lockshoek (Free State and Karoo South Africa) and Pomongwan (Matobo Zimbabwe)."}

{"id": "bc373cce-b592-40c3-9ad1-3c563533196f", "value": "The final period of the Stone Age dating from around 40 000 years ago BP and into the historic period ending at various times in different regions in southern Africa. Assemblages are generally microlithic in character and include a wide range of organic and inorganic artefacts. Three Later Stone Age (LSA) industries occur - Late Pleistocene Microlithic (18000 - 12000 BP) Oakhurst (12000 - 7000 BP) and Wilton (8000 - 100 BP) each of which carry different regional variations. The LSA is also characterised by the high variability in settlement patterns subsistence strategies and social organisation across different regions of southern Africa. Evidence for burials the use of personal ornamentation and exchange networks are identified. The production of rock art in the form of paintings and engravings are widely evidenced across the the region. The Ceramic Later Stone Age phase occurs within the last 2000 years BP and generally co-occurs with the introduction of the first domestic livestock. The final Later Stone Age overlaps with the presence of the farming communities and later Europeans on the landscape. Use more specific type where known. | Definition 1: Part of the Late Holocene/ Final Later Stone Age of Southern Africa ceramic assemblages often thin-walled either organic (grass shell) or mineral-tempered begin to appear in the excavated record at multiple sites in different regions and dating from around 2000 BP up to the recent past. These ceramic assemblages often co-occur within microlithic assemblages. Regional variants include Cape coastal Pottery (southern and Western Cape South Africa) Smithfield B (Seacow River Valley South Africa) Doornfontein (Northern Cape South Africa) Bambata A (Zimbabwe and Botswana) Gwanda Ware or Matopan Ceramic phase in Zimbabwe. Dates for the ceramic Later Stone Age in Southern Africa vary from c. 26 BCE up to around the 19th century as recorded by early travellers along the Western Cape coast of Southern Africa. Definition 2: Later Stone Age ceramics predate Iron Age wares by as much as four centuries and this not only in the southeast. These Later Stone Age pots are quite distinct from Iron Age ware which is mineral tempered thick-walled (generally over 10 mm thick) with a coarse surface texture. By contrast the earliest pots from Later Stone Age sites are considerably thinner (five or six mm average wall thickness slightly thicker in the southeastern parts of the subcontinent) with mostly smooth and often burnished surfaces. Some are tempered with organic materials such as grass and charcoal. | Bambata type A pottery is often characterised as thin-walled around 4-6mm thick and well fired. Pottery shapes mostly occur in the form of jars necked vessels and bowls Outer surface of sherds have a black to grey appearance and can be heavily decorated with multiple bands of alternating designs with comb-stamping being and broad incision. The pottery is described as charcoal tempered. A few spouts have also been identified as part of the ceramic assemblage. The pottery has been identified at sites in Botswana near Lake Ngami extending along Boteti and towards the Makgadikgadi Pans around the Matobo region of Zimbabwe (referred to as Gwanda ceramics) as well as into the northern parts of South Africa in the Limpopo Basin. There are few dates associated with this type of pottery but occurs within the early part of the first millennium CE. The makers of Bambata type A pottery are debated particularly whether such ceramics were an indigenous local southern African innovation amongst hunting and gathering/fisher communities or whether they were made by early farmers speaking an Eastern or Western Bantu-language. Alternatively the pottery could also be atttibuted to Khoe-speaking pastoralists. The ceramic assemblages have been suggested to be distinct from a thicker-walled Bambata Type B ceramic generally associated within Early Farming Community contexts in southern Africa."}

{"id": "adb49f25-2ad0-499c-b3e8-bb2bf9be701d", "value": "Definition 1: The Robberg industry is the earliest tecnological expression of the Later Stone Age. In the southern Cape of South Africa it dates to the end of the Late Pleistocene between 24 000 and 12 000 years ago. The industry is characterised by a few backed tools and scrapers. It has also been found further afield in the Free State Province of South Africa and Lesotho. Definition 2: The upper boundary of the Early LSA is capped by the Robberg Industry (Deacon1984ab).Robberg assemblages also known as the Early Microlithic (Mitchell1988)were identified first at Nelson Bay Cave and other nearby sites such as Melkhoutboom (Klein 1972 Deacon19761978). The Robberg is characterized by the systematic production of microlithic bladelets and a dearth of formal tools (Deacon1984ab)."}

{"id": "cdb5ec55-4f7d-4bf0-8151-b6bf5ffb2a88", "value": "The Maleme Industry refers to mircolithic assemblages recovered from sites in the Matobo region of Zimbabwe. It is one of the first definite Later Stone Age industries to have been identified in the region. Dating between 13 000 to 11 000 years ago this industry is characterised by microlithic scrapers few prepared microlithic cores and triangular points and awls. The industry also contains evidence of bone cylinder beads and ornaments."}

{"id": "1296f147-1111-48f8-a5b4-2132e823cfa2", "value": "An industry of that follows and partially overlaps the Southern African and Eastern African Later Stone Age and has three broad phases: Nachikufan 1 (c. 16700 to 10800 BP) Nachikufan 2 (c. 9700--5000 B.P) Nachikufan 3 (c. 3500--200 B.P.). All known Nachikufan sites are found in Zambia. They lie north of the Zambezi river mostly west of the Luangwa river and primarily east of the Kafue river. | Follows and partially overlaps with the Southern and Eastern Africa Later Stone Age tradition and occurs north of the Zambezi River. Nachikufan 1 has been identified as the earliest phase of the Nachikufan industry and is estimated to date between 16700 to 10800 BP."}

{"id": "1aef117e-9797-42f1-9985-547c263f0053", "value": "An industry of the Later Stone Age dating between 18000 to 12000 years ago BP. Lithic assemblages are characterised as microlithic rich in unmodified bladelets and bladelets. Few formal tools are reported. The industry is present predominantly in eastern Zimbabwe and known from the site Duncombe Farm however it is understood to have closer affinities to the Nachikufu 1 industry in Zambia. Late Pleistocene Microlithic is documented as Robberg in South Africa."}

{"id": "cda97c22-06bd-4a2b-bd56-18ba9ac20dbe", "value": "A technocomplex of the Holocene/Later Stone Age often referred to as the Post-classic Wilton and dating from roughly 4000 years ago BP. Assemblages are characterised as highly variable. Worked bone ostrich eggshell and ochre are commonly found in assemblages. Regional variants include Smithfield (Karoo Free-State South Africa) Kablejous (Northern Cape South Africa) and Amazimba (Zimbabwe). Use more specific type where known. | An industry of the Later Stone Age occuring predominantly in the Matobo region of Zimbabwe. The industry is characterised by a proliferation of bone tools tranchets shale pendants ostrich egg shell containers bone link shafts bone points and drilled bone disc beads."}

{"id": "79bbe16b-7525-4252-b02f-206bbc3e17c3", "value": "Definition 1: A lithic technocomplex dating from around 40 kya to 18 kya and relates to a transition or overlap between the Middle Stone Age (MSA) and Later Stone Age (LSA) in southern Africa. Assemblages are characterised by unstandardised often microlithic stone tools that generally occur before 20 000 years ago BP. In Zimbabwe the transition from MSA to LSA has been referred to as the Tshangula Industry (associated with final Middle Stone Age). Definition 2: ELSA is characterised by large scrapers including circular convex concave and informal types scaled pieces broad irregular flakes and micro-blades with predominantly plain striking platforms."}

{"id": "8db0ea3a-9496-4c1b-a95d-bf2cd1e86c62", "value": "An independent kingdom native to Kush (Nubia) emerging after the end of the Egyptian New Kingdom occupation in the Middle Nile Region and existing as a political unit until the AD 5th century. | Period of Kushite dynasty in which the kings of Kush were buried at Napata on the Fourth Cataract. The first part of this period during the 25th Dynasty in Egypt is distinct in a variety of ways from the rest of this period and so is sometimes considered not part of the Napatan period but as it sometimes is it is included within this period. | Sudan Lower Wadi Howar Gala Abu Ahmed fortress"}

{"id": "312533e6-36d3-4e2e-a9e7-4deb5460cbe6", "value": "Description: So in conclusion it is evident that the non-microlithic industries of the Terminal Pleistocene and Holocene of West Africa comprise essentially three broad types: 1. Predominantly plain platform prepared core and/or macroflake industries occurring without associated microliths from the Terminal Pleistocene until as recently as 6000 bp. 2. Predominantly faceted platform ('Levallois') industries occurring in association with non-geometric microliths and dating from cal0000 to 4000 bp and 3. 'Core Tool' components of Late Stone Age 'Neolithic' or even Iron Age cultures usually already possessing ceramics and dating to between ca 6000 and 1500 bp. Such pieces constitute the totality of many factories site assemblages but are also present as a component of more varied assemblages at habitation sites. The polishing of these chipped 'roughouts' would appear to be a later development which did not become common until sometime after 4500 bp."}

{"id": "f112d8a9-4b60-40e9-bb33-6437ef2565b6", "value": "A broader term for the Bronze Age period within Upper Nubia generally defined by the Kerma culture and its precursor the Pre-Kerma. The Kerma (although possibly not the Pre-Kerma) is also defined as part of a broader Kingdom of Kush the first polity referred to as such but due to the discontinuity between this Kingdom and the later Kingdom of Kush centred around Napata and Meroe they have been defined separately here. 3500BCE - 1450 BCE. | The Pre-Kerma is a cultural period in Upper Nubia preceding the Kerma civilisation and with many similar characteristics. It also has some similarities to the A-Group of Lower Nubia especially regarding pottery. | First period of Kerman culture. Territorial authority seemingly divided but with Kerma itself as leading power. May have been the period during which the great Deffufa was built at Kerma (Bonnet 2004). Also known as Kerma Ancien."}

{"id": "b8786112-cf0a-490f-b470-3e005c6c0c30", "value": "Definition 1: The kingdom of Kerma is a political entity which dominated Upper Nubia from ca. 2500 to 1500 BC. Its political centre is the city of Kerma which has extensive fortification and ritual buildings. Egypt conquers the kingdom of Kerma in the 18th dynasty after several campaigns. Around 1500 BC Kerma is destroyed and its burial ground is deserted. Definition 2: A culture based around the site of Kerma (named after a modern village in the same location) generally regarded as a precursor to the later Kingdom of Kush. It has multiple sub-periods. The central site of Kerma was eventually destroyed in the 15th century BC. | Third period of Kerman culture simultaneous with rise of First Empire of Kush. Also known as Kerma Classique."}

{"id": "777fe014-c88b-42f0-b529-126559a36453", "value": "Urewe pottery is named after the site type in Western Kenya. It was originally named dimple-based ware due to the thumb sized impression in the centers of the base. The pottery has thick beveled rims which are often incised or grooved and the assemblage consists of necked pots and shallow hemispheric bowls with a dimpled base. This pottery is heavily decorated but the decorations do not cover the entire body. The basic motif is parallel grooved or incised bands around the shoulder and body that often incorporates circles loops and triangles. Hatching and dots are often found on or just below the rim. Urewe pottery is found in the great lakes region from Kivu in the west to the eastern shores of Lake Victoria from the Chobi area of Uganda to the southern shores of Lake Victoria and into Burundi. The pottery is almost always found in association with iron working and never with lithics and was eventually replaced by rouletted pottery beginning AD 1000. 2600-1300 BP/ 550BC-650 AD"}

{"id": "62cdc094-cc06-4f0d-b083-017682f3e634", "value": "Early Iron Age pottery of the Chifumbaze Complex from central Tanzania this pottery is typologically intermediate between Urewe and Kwale wares. It has been found in the areas around L Eyasiand and Sandaweland. 246-338CE"}

{"id": "43b49f81-9250-4c29-bdff-7fed96cb1fea", "value": "Period when farming communities started making and using iron tools. Period mainly represented by pottery wares such as Urewe that were associated with farming communities.2600BP-1600CE. | Pottery with thickened rims and bevels or flutes on pots or bowls. Hatched or grooved bands on shoulder of pots or below shoulder on bowls. Occurs in S.E. Kenya and the highlands of N.E. Tanzania"}

{"id": "a2c05c40-6ea6-42aa-9382-099551ba9066", "value": "Christianity has tended to dominate narratives of medieval Ethiopia because of its long history and links with the Solomonic Dynasty which reigned from the late thirteenth century. {"id": "a0bb2104-5110-49f0-9f54-8adebb820ef5", "value": "Stone flaking technologies associated with hunter gatherer economy highly mobile populations lacking pottery exploited range of habitats and a variety of medium to large sized animals and who participated in wide ranging exchange networks that gave them access to different lithic materials such as obsidian and chert. {"id": "2113d7bd-b821-4291-a639-1a9e09f9e0d2", "value": "Recorded at the site Diallowalli the pottery of this phase is of small or medium size and the paste is fine. {"id": "b703b948-899e-4e22-8d82-d28cb805be7d", "value": "Description: The ceramics of the Wind\u00e9 Koroji tradition are characterized by numerous shallow cauldrons and tighly closed jars both featuring everted rims (fig. 4a-c). Alo distinctive but much less common are broad basins (fig. 4d). Open bowls and globular simple rimmed vessels are also present (fig. 4e-f). The most common decors are twisted twine roulettes (Twisted Tw) impressed or roulette cord-wrapped stick (ICS/CSR) and impressed netting (Net/Fabric) (Table 1). The latter motif is especially striking occurring both tightly applied to the vessel and loosely impressed. Highly distinctive but less common decor types include knotted twine roulettes (often featuring multiple knots) (fig. 4c) braided twine roulette (which produce a herringbone effect) and a curious type of applied plastic decor. This latter motif features the semi-perforation of the pot with a blunt tipped object and a subsequent re-finishing of resultant voids and bulbs (fig. 4d). The site of Wind\u00e9 Koroji Ouest (WKO) the type site of the facies is located at the centre of the Wind\u00e9 Koroji complex in the vicinity of a seasonal Songhai hamlet. | Description: Le faci\u00e8s de Wind\u00e9 Koroji bien qu'apparent\u00e9 aux faci\u00e8s n\u00e9olithiques de la vall\u00e9e du Tilemsi offre plusieurs particularit\u00e9s. Il se caract\u00e9rise au niveau de la c\u00e9ramique par des formes en chaudrons peu profonds et des jarres \u00e0 ouverture r\u00e9duite. La plupart des bords sont assez \u00e9vers\u00e9s. Les poteries sont en r\u00e8gle g\u00e9n\u00e9rale d\u00e9graiss\u00e9es \u00e0 la chamotte et d\u00e9cor\u00e9es au peigne filet\u00e9 souple \u00e0 la cordelette roul\u00e9e ou bien encore par impression de nattes ou de filets. L'industrie lithique est tr\u00e8s particuli\u00e8re. Les armatiures de fl\u00e8ches salicyforme ou foliac\u00e9es en silex pr\u00e9dominent au c\u00f4t\u00e9 d'une industrie grossi\u00e8re sur gr\u00e8s. Les haches polies de tailles variable sont aussi pr\u00e9sentes. Les sondages sir me soye de Wind\u00e9 Koroji ont r\u00e9v\u00e9l\u00e9 deux structures pratiquement affleurante : le fond d'une hutte circulaire et une petite fosse remple de mat\u00e9riel. Les restes de faune comprennent des bovins des ovicaprins un grand nombre de mammif\u00e8res sauvages et des poissons adapt\u00e9s aux eaux peu profondes. Les meules sont abondantes. Les restes de pal\u00e9oflore ont livr\u00e9 des esp\u00e8ces sauvages et quelques graines de Pennisetim sp. vraisemblablement domestique. Une \u00e9conomie pastorale semble pouvoir \u00eatre rattach\u00e9e au faci\u00e8s Wind\u00e9 Koroji."}

{"id": "f7f160fc-c1e3-4891-a966-c83f59325301", "value": "Within the early parts of the second millennium AD the appearance of pierced lugs (possibly used for suspension purposes) are evidenced in the archaeological record for southwestern Southern Africa particularly along the southwestern Cape coast of South Africa and Namibia and to a lesser extent further inland. Reports of lugged ware from northern Botswana have also been described but remain undated. The ware is commonly referred to as \u2018Khoe\u2019 or \u2018Khoi\u2019 pottery as documented during the 17th Century by early European vistitors at the Cape and attributed to historical Khoekhoen. The pottery is characterised as being coil built mineral-tempered (sometimes quartz inclusion) a shouldered-jar form with suspension lugs a neck and everted lip having a general amphora-like shape although it is suggested that there is much diversity in the morphology of lugged ware."}

{"id": "ea3620b0-38bb-428d-863b-cd77c2431a4d", "value": "The term refers to a unit defining a major block of time in archaeology and may contain several phases over a wide geographic area. he concepts around periodisation were originally developed by the European three-age system (Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age).The concepts around periodisation were originally developed by the European three-age system (Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age) based on the concept of 'progress'.Although such terms (albeit refined) are still widely referred to in the archaeology of non-western regions today, there remain several debates about their usefulness for understanding the past both in terms of temporality and historicity. Most commonly used terms in African archaeological literature include periods such as the Stone Age, Paeolithic, Neolithic, Iron Age, Historical Period (etc) and can be divided into broader temporal units relating to the pre-historic or historic past and/or the pre-colonial or colonial past, each of which carries underlying assumptions and compartmentalisations of the past (for full reviews see Hall, M. and Silliman, S.W., 2006. Introduction: Archaeology of the modern world. In Historical Archaeology. Hall, M. and Silliman, S.W. (eds). Oxford: Blackwell Publishing, Schmidt, P.R., Pikirayi, I. Will Historical Archaeology Escape Its Western Prejudices to Become Relevant to Africa?. Arch 14, 443\u2013471 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11759-018-9342-1 , Connah, G. (2007). Historical archaeology in Africa: An appropriate concept? African Archaeological Review, 1\u20132, 35\u201340. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10437-007-9014-9 , Lightfoot, K. G. (1995). Culture contact studies: Redefining the relationship between prehistoric and historical archaeology. American Antiquity, 60(2), 199\u2013217. https://doi.org/10.2307/282137 , Reid, A. M., & Lane, P. J. (Eds.) (2004). African historical archaeologies. New York: Academic. and Karega-Munene, and Peter Schmidt. \u201cPostcolonial Archaeologies in Africa: Breaking the Silence.\u201d The African Archaeological Review 27, no. 4 (2010): 323\u201337. http://www.jstor.org/stable/40930993 with references therein)."}

{"id": "a0719c16-8fa9-4181-82fb-87029b0d6963", "value": "A politically independent or autonomous social unit, whether simple or complex. In the case of a complex society, such as a state, it may comprise many dependent components. The Polity concept can be used when the chronology resource entry has been characterised by the reign of a particular empire, kingdom, dyastry, state and/or complex society over a particular timespan."}

{"id": "8b0d60a5-c5d3-44ef-84c3-ea11ad431e7f", "value": "The Late Stone Age (LSA) is characterised by the appearance of much smaller tools known as microliths often in standardized geometric forms. Elsewhere in Africa these technologies appear around thirty kya but in the Senegambia they do so significantly later (fifteen to ten ka) shortly before the use of ceramics and the development of agriculture. The earliest conclusive evidence of LSA technologies comes from the site of Tomboura 1 in the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 region which has yielded dates going back to approximately 15 ka."}

{"id": "a60a2b7b-ce20-4b38-9a4a-38970616d022", "value": "The Late Stone Age (LSA) is characterised by the appearance of much smaller tools known as microliths often in standardized geometric forms. The tools only occur in the area east of Lake Turkana in sites in the Karari escarpment."}

{"id": "8f49e01b-c158-4ced-86d6-d142fdcaf7f9", "value": "Term suggested for a period that is represented by tools at least 700000 years before the earliest Oldowan tools in Eastern Africa. They have only been found at one site west of Lake Turkana Lomekwi 3. Assembalage composed of cores and flakes the cores being made from heavy large sized pebbles. The flake production technique is described as a combination of core reduction and battering activities by passive hammer and bipolar mainly by freehand percussion. There is much debate about who made these tools since Australopithecines and Homo lived here at this time."}

{"id": "af5d8979-afba-4b83-8337-35215325461b", "value": "The process by which land is covered by continental and alpine glacier ice sheets or the period of time during which such covering occurred; several glaciations are required to make up an Ice Age (as the Pleistocene). The land is subject to erosion and deposition by this process, which occurred repeatedly during the Quaternary; the process modifies landscapes and affects the level of ocean basins. These periods of colder weather are also called glacials, and the warmer periods between them interglacials."}

{"id": "f52edd91-4226-4123-8db2-194b1b0a1e2f", "value": "A geological event is a temporally and spatially heterogeneous and dynamic (diachronous) episode in Earth history that contributes to the transformation of Earth system and the formation of geological strata. Event stratigraphy was first proposed as a system for the recognition, study and correlation of the effects of important physical or biological events on the broader stratigraphical record. Geological events as a chronology type may refer to particular glaciation events and stages, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes or other key geological events shaping earth's history"}

{"id": "a1ab2864-1a9a-495a-bb9d-8f87f0ce4fcc", "value": "The second epoch of the Quaternary and the most recent geologic interval of time. The name which means \u2018entirely recent' extends from about 11 700 BCE to the present. It coincides with the late and post-Stone Age history of the human species . It is also associated with the current interglacial (~11 700 BP - present day). Holocene stratigraphic records provide evidence inter alia of climate and sea-level change geomorphological and hydrological processes vegetational developments and faunal migrations. In addition they contain a unique range and wealth of archaeological data that attest to the development of society and the evolving relationships between people and the environment under near modern boundary conditions. | An informal tripartite subdivision of the Holocene that has long been employed and describes the earliest of three formally defined chronostratigraphic and geochronological units: the Lower/Early Middle and Upper/Late Holocene subseries/subepochs. This first stage/age of the Holocene is also termed the Greenlandian Stage/Age with its GSSP in the Greenland NGRIP2 ice core and dated at 11700 yr b2k (before 2000 CE) and is defined with its corrresponding Early Holocene Subseries/Subepoch.This subdivision was formally ratified by the Executive Committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) on 14th June 2018. | A stadial of the Weichselian cold stage dated to between 11000 and 10000BP. The last glacial recession (13000\u20136000 years ago) was interrupted by this sharp advance. It takes its name from a tundra plant called Dryas octopetala."}

{"id": "a7b72e7a-b439-4a34-ad97-78d6140129cf", "value": "Marine Isotope Stage 2 of the Upper/Late Pleniglacial. Characterised by the coldest period of the last glacial cycle with sea levels dropping and generally drier conditions than present-day. Occurs around 29 - 14 kya during the Late Pleistocene. Also referred to the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM). The Middle Stone Age disappears."}

{"id": "e411ae19-28d6-40ac-aa3a-fdd8f0f9cb6c", "value": "Description: The Kobadi tradition would appear to have been of an entirely fisher-hunter-gatherer economic orientation and has been documented in the Malian Sahara and throughout most of the Middle Niger and Niger bend area (e.g. Raimbault and Dutour 1989 Togola and Raimbault 1991 MacDonald and Van Neer 1994 MacDonald 1996b Raimbault 1996). Kobadi ceramics differ greatly from those of Tichitt having entirely different rim forms (simple rather than everted) decorative tools (comb and spatula rather than cordwrapped stick) and fabric (sand and sponge temper rather than chaff)."}

{"id": "7465a6e9-fc38-4211-b5cc-1c901bf864c9", "value": "The Neolithic period extends from 6185 to 2000BC. Its sites are spread throughout Senegal. In general they are found on the slopes of the Ogolian dunes the Grande C\u00f4te Dakar and Saint Louis. There are also numerous sites on the continental plain particularly in the center of the country (the Ferlo) and in the valleys of the Senegal and Gambia rivers as well as their main tributaries. These sites are located in varied microclimates. This variability indicates different modes of adaptation including subsistence strategies that have been adapted to varied environments where specific lithic (macro or microlithic) ceramic or bone technologies flourished. | This facies eponymous with the Cap Manuel site has a chronology between 5434 and 411 BC. The material culture is essentially characterised by lithic and ceramic remains. The lithics consist of macro-tools such as strikers nuclei elongated pieces and nucleiform planes. Ceramics which are rare are tempered by quartz laterite and gravel. The decoration consists of impressions made with a threaded comb or rolled cord."}

{"id": "f609cf2b-4c96-49f9-88ac-019c48999c13", "value": "A technique which uses the measurement of decay in radioactive lead (Pb) isotopes to determine a date. Useful for sediments and lead-based paints between 1 and 400 years old."}

{"id": "b307e831-5068-43f2-a214-783fb3a8aa12", "value": "Definition 1: Last Interglacial with temperatures slightly warmer and slightly higher sea levels. 130 - 117 kya. Possible Homo sapiens migration out-of-Africa. Definition 2: The last interglacial of northern Europe after the Saalian and before the Weichsel Glaciation from c 125000\u2013115000 BP. This group of Quarternary interglacial deposits are found right across Europe from the Netherlands to Russia and contain fossils that indicate warm conditions. In the Netherlands and northern Germany the rising sea level caused the deposition of Eemian marine sediments. Evidence from bore holes indicates that the Eemian may represent two or even three interglacial stages. Levalloisian and Mousterian artifacts are found in Eemina deposits."}

{"id": "95422e2b-35e5-491f-ac06-76d82cffee82", "value": "A lithic industry transitional from the Earlier Stone Age to the early Middle Stone Age and appears to occur south of the LImpopo in South Africa. It includes prepared cores blades and very reduced numbers of large cutting tools compared with the Acheulean and it often includes convergent flakes and retouched pointsprepared cores (Levoill blades and very reduced numbers of large cutting tools compared with the Acheulean The term is debated with some researchers suggesting to subsume it within the Later final Achuelean in southern Africa. The industry is dated roughly around ca. ~ 600 to 200 ka."}

{"id": "f0896c02-e37e-472c-a9e1-d4387e653a2a", "value": "A transitional period from Earlier Stone Age (ESA) to the Middle Stone Age (MSA). The period is generally defined as a change in use of large cutting tools (LCTs) such as handaxes and cleavers to the use of blades points and prepared core technology (Levallois). In southern Africa some researchers identify transitional industries such as the Fauresmith (South Africa) and Sangoan (Zambia) as a transitional industry developed out of the Later Final Acheulean. Date range: ~ 600 - 200 kya. Use more specific type where known. | Bambesi (alt. Sangoan) is considered to be a transitional lithic industry between the Later Achuelean and the early Middle Stone Age."}

{"id": "51852606-de04-4502-9947-7e185d78bad9", "value": "The Sangoan industry (referred to as Bambesi in Zimbabwe) is considered to be a transitional lithic industry between the Later Achuelean and the early Middle Stone Age deriving predominantly north of the Limpopo River basin in southern Africa. It has been described from the Kalambo Falls site of Zambia and at sites Hope Fountain Pomongwe Bambata and Gweru Kopje and other sites around Hwange National Park Zimbabwe. The industry is characterised by the low presense of prepared cores that are absent from the Later Achuelean and by the presence of rare handaxes and cleavers core-axes core-scrapers and blade cores. Sangoan Industry is roughly thought to date from around ca. 500 - 300 ka."}

{"id": "abce2cf6-b3c2-43f6-94eb-5d95d47ee70e", "value": "An industry of that follows and partially overlaps the Southern African and Eastern African Later Stone Age and has three broad phases: Nachikufan 1 (c. 16700 to 10800 BP) Nachikufan 2 (c. 9700-5000 B.P) Nachikufan 3 (c. 3500-200 B.P.). All known Nachikufan sites are found in Zambia. They lie north of the Zambezi river mostly west of the Luangwa river and primarily east of the Kafue river."}

{"id": "d4db6d51-b576-4607-9125-89c4c25dfeac", "value": "Pottery whose decoration was executed with catfish spine or mollusc shell imitating basketry such as those used for fishing. It appeared at waterside sites around 6000BC occuring from the Kenyan rift valley to the western Sahara during the period when lake levels were high. The pottery is often but not always found in association with fishing barbed points. Fish remains common. 7th-2nd mill BC"}

{"id": "daf8eec6-244f-469f-abb2-f520e550a450", "value": "The most striking marker of this period is the widespread use of bone to produce standardised artifact types known as points. LSA is also associated with the manufacture of art objects and ornaments especially beads and pendants made in bone and shell inclduing ostritch eggshell beads | The LSA in Ethiopia is characterised with the development of a microlithic industry. Many terminologies have been applied to this period including the Mode4/5 Industry Blade Mode 4 Industry as well as the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition which has been divided into three discrete temporal phases. Currently the earliest date for the start of the LSA in Ethiopia is 27 kya. Evidence indicates that microlithic tools were being manufactured well within the Aksumite Period in the form of highly standardised scrapers. Microlithic technologies also co-occur with the first evidence of pottery in northern Ethiopia dated to around 4700 years ago and with the presence of domestic livestock in the faunal remains. The industry also co-occurs with the presence of grindstones and later with classical and late Aksumite pottery dating from the fifth to sixth centuries AD. | Based on Brandt (1980) and Clark and Williams (1978) classification of the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition phase A refers to a transitional and emergent microlithic industry characterised by the use of local obsidian on backed geometric microliths and scrapers. Date range: 22 to 19 kya. The start date should be taken as tentative as the radiocarbon date from which it derives is made on ostrich eggshell. Note that this phase has been based on research conducted in and around Lake Besaka Rift Valley Ethiopia."}

{"id": "dea0e82d-7aad-4891-9505-177e21aba402", "value": "The most striking marker of this period is the widespread use of bone to produce standardised artifact types known as points. LSA is also associated with the manufacture of art objects and ornaments especially beads and pendants made in bone and shell inclduing ostritch eggshell beads | The LSA in Ethiopia is characterised with the development of a microlithic industry. Many terminologies have been applied to this period including the Mode4/5 Industry Blade Mode 4 Industry as well as the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition which has been divided into three discrete temporal phases. Currently the earliest date for the start of the LSA in Ethiopia is 27 kya. Evidence indicates that microlithic tools were being manufactured well within the Aksumite Period in the form of highly standardised scrapers. Microlithic technologies also co-occur with the first evidence of pottery in northern Ethiopia dated to around 4700 years ago and with the presence of domestic livestock in the faunal remains. The industry also co-occurs with the presence of grindstones and later with classical and late Aksumite pottery dating from the fifth to sixth centuries AD. | Based on Brandt (1980) and Clark and Williams (1978) classification of the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition phase A refers to a transitional and emergent microlithic industry characterised by the use of local obsidian on backed geometric microliths and scrapers. {"id": "039025fb-8e95-496e-867c-7a10ea848590", "value": "The African Stone Age spans the first 2.5 Ma of human prehistory beginning with the world\u2019s earliest stone tool production and continuing through the historical period of European colonization. The African Stone Age includes a tremendous diversity in terms of the characteristics of its industries and the life ways engaged in by its makers. Archaeological research on African stone tool industries has had wide-ranging impacts on our understanding of processes of human evolution and the organization of past human societies. The Stone Age conventionally encompasses three broad phases: Early Stone Age (ESA) Middle Stone Age (MSA) and Later Stone Age (LSA). Use more specific type where known. | This is the first and earliest period of the Stone Age occuring during the Plio-Pleistocene and dating from 2.1 mya to 0.2 mya for southern Africa. The Early Stone Age is characterised by the oldest known cultural material produced by hominins and is generally characterised by simple stone tool industries including the Oldowan dating between 2.1 mya and 1.7 mya and the Acheulean dating between 1.4 mya and 0.2 mya . In Southern Africa the earliest stone tools include simple flakes struck from cobbles core and pebble tools and in later stages include intentionally shaped handaxes cleavers and picks final or transitional stages have tools that are smaller than the preceding stages and include large blades. Use more specific type where known. | The longest lasting industry of the Plio-Pleistocene/Early Stone Age in southern Africa and dating from about 1.3 mya to around 250 kya. It is marked by the presence of bifacial implements predominantly handaxes and cleavers that are made on a variety of stone materials. A continuation of simple tool forms including cores and flakes from the Oldowan is evidenced however retouched flakes become more common. Earliest and most securely dated evidence for this industry derives from Ethiopia."}

All known Nachikufan sites are found in Zambia. They lie north of the Zambezi river mostly west of the Luangwa river and primarily east of the Kafue river."}

{"id": "424282ab-aaed-4c1f-831e-3e751a5a7909", "value": "The Aksumite Culture has a ceramic tradition which is widespread in central Tigray. It begins with an early phase which dates before the political unit which we know from written sources. The ceramic tradition of central Tigray (c. 1000 BC\u2013AD 700) is represented by several sites around Yeha and Aksum (Michels 2005 Sernicola 2008). This region has been more extensively investigated and a reasonably solid cultural sequence has been outlined from the combined results of the stratigraphic sequence of the ceramics radiocarbon dating of almost fifty charcoal samples cross-dating on fragments of foreign vases and glass artefacts and coins. | Classic Aksumite phase ceramic assemblages are characterized by round basins with a ledge rim and foot-rings globular jars with high neck small bowls with foot-rings and a ledge rim often decorated with vertical corrugations alternating with bands of incised diamonds. | King of Aksumite prior to mid-6th century AD"}

{"id": "3962699d-ed4a-4669-9b33-0228034a1f1d", "value": "This is an intermediate industry between the Acheulean and the Middle Stone Age thought to be an adaptation to a forested environment. The assemblage is characterized by tools that seem to signal a transition between the above industries. Although usually grouped together descriptions of the Sangoan-Lupemban are slightly different with the former having both heavy duty and light duty tools scrapers utilised and retouched tools while the Lupemban consists of points foliate shaped lanceolate and Levallois debitage. Dating still problematic."}

{"id": "d74a3057-ee40-4abd-992e-2f9a6b642fcb", "value": "Regional subtradition of the Pastoral Neolithic the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic (SPN) encompasses sites with a predominately domestic fauna associated with a wide range of ceramic styles including Narosura Nderit Ileret Akira and Maringishu a preference for grey-hued obsidians sourced to the Lake Naivasha Basin particular lithic production techniques and tool styles cairn burials and settlement in highland and lowland savannas. 5000-1300BP | Sites found in central Kenya to northern Tanzania in areas above 1500m asl. 3300-1300BP | This pottery tradition has ceramics associated with stone bowls pestles axes cattle- and caprine-based economies as well as diverse stone artefacts and large settlements dating to 2nd millennium BCE and 10th century CE around the Central Rift south to Eyasi east to Tsavo (coastal hinterland) and the Serengeti-Mara Plains. 1900-1200BP"}

{"id": "df664443-7069-49f2-a8a9-d7954c80806b", "value": "Around the transition between the first and second millennium CE is a period widely referred to as the Medieval Climate Anomaly. Hemisphere-wide and global syntheses suggest that this period was generally warmer than the subsequent Little Ice Age. Tyson et al. (2000) suggest that warming may have increased by as much as ~+3\u00b0C south of Lake Malawi. The timing and spatial variability of the MCA is considered to be highly complex with high resolution records being comparatively patchy in terms of geographical coverage across Africa. General synthesis indicates that the MCA was wetter than today across the Sahel. In the more humid regions south of the Sahel the MCA has been suggested to be relatively arid with sites across East Africa from Ethopia to northern Malawi being drier than average. In Southern African records indicate that the period is characterised generally by increased humidity and warm conditions between 900 CE and 1250 and were interrupted by significantly drier conditions at around c. 1200 CE although on the southeastern side of southern Africa records seem to show greater variability (see also Nash 2016 for an overview)."}

{"id": "959f002d-fc33-42d8-8ce0-b42ea6b49348", "value": "An informal tripartite subdivision of the Holocene that has long been employed and describes the latest of three formally defined chronostratigraphic and geochronological units: the Lower/Early Middle and Upper/Late Holocene subseries/subepochs. This uppermost subdividion of the Holocene is also termed the Meghalayan Stage/Age with its GSSP in a speleothem from Mawmluh Cave northeastern India with a date of 4250 yr b2k (before 2000 CE) indicating a global marked reduction in rainfall. This subdivision was formally ratified by the Executive Committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) on 14th June 2018. | A recent glacial stage called the Little Ice Age began in the sixteenth century and advanced and receded intermittently over three centuries. Its maximum development was reached about 1750 at which time glaciers were more widespread on Earth than at any time since the principal Quaternary Ice Ages."}

{"id": "03fe028a-dcb6-4a27-ad67-6e934e616eeb", "value": "This symmetric property associates an instance of E53 Place with another instance of E53 Place which shares a part of its border. This property is purely spatial. It does not imply that the phenomena that define, by their extent, places related by P122 borders with have ever shared a respective border at the same time or even coexisted. In particular, this may be the case when the respective common border is formed by a natural feature. This property is not transitive. This property is symmetric."}

{"id": "544ecc76-9fe3-4c8b-9f14-acceb5e71a29", "value": "This property describes the largest volume in space, an instance of E53 Place, that an instance of E18 Physical Thing has occupied at any time during its existence, with respect to the reference space relative to the physical thing itself. This allows for describing the thing itself as a place that may contain other things, such as a box that may contain coins. In other words, it is the volume that contains all the points which the thing has covered at some time during its existence. The reference space for the associated place must be the one that is permanently at rest (P157 is at rest relative to (provides reference space for)) relative to the physical thing. For instances of E19 Physical Objects it is the one which is at rest relative to the object itself, i.e., which moves together with the object. For instances of E26 Physical Feature it is one which is at rest relative to the physical feature itself and the surrounding matter immediately connected to it. Therefore, there is a 1:1 relation between the instance E18 Physical Thing and the instance of E53 Place it occupies. We include in the occupied space the space filled by the matter of the physical thing and all its inner spaces. This property is equivalent to the fully developed path from E18 Physical Thing through P196 defines, E92 Spacetime Volume, P161 has spatial projection (is spatial projection of) to E53 Place. However, in contrast to P156 occupies (is occupied by), the property P161 has spatial projection (is spatial projection of) does not constrain the reference space of the referred instance of E53 Place. It does not constrain the reference space of the referred instance of E53 Place. It identifies a possibly wider instance of E53 Place at which a thing is or has been for some unspecified time-span. If the reference space of the referred instance of E53 Place is not at rest with respect to the physical thing found there, the physical thing may move away after some time to another place and/or may have been at some other place before. The same holds for the fully developed path from E18 Physical Thing through P196 defines (is defined by), E92 Spacetime Volume, P161 has spatial projection (is spatial projection of) to E53 Place."}

{"id": "4f0fca17-cd8a-457c-b43f-f85a63b2efec", "value": "This property documents the number of parts, an instance of E60 Number, of which an instance of E19 Physical Object is composed. This may be used as a method of checking inventory counts with regard to aggregate or collective objects. What constitutes a part or component depends on the context and requirements of the documentation. Normally, the parts documented in this way would not be considered as worthy of individual attention. For a more complete description, objects may be decomposed into their components and constituents using P46 is composed of (forms parts of) and P45 consists of (is incorporated in). This allows each element to be described individually."}

{"id": "ee27d893-b702-4d02-a877-46f2dd457cf4", "value": "This property associates an instance of E53 Place with another instance of E53 Place, which is defined in the same reference space, and which is used to approximate the former. The property does not necessarily state the quality or accuracy of this approximation, but rather indicates the use of the first instance of place to approximate the second. In common documentation practice, find or encounter spots e.g., in archaeology, botany or zoology are often related to the closest village, river or other named place without detailing the relation, e.g., if it is located within the village or in a certain distance of the specified place. In this case the stated \u201cphenomenal\u201d place found in the documentation can be seen as an approximation of the actual encounter spot without more specific knowledge. In more recent documentation often point coordinate information is provided that originates from GPS measurements or georeferencing from a map. This point coordinate information does not state the actual place of the encounter spot but tries to approximate it with a \u201cdeclarative\u201d place. The accuracy depends on the methodology used when creating the coordinates. It may be dependent on technical limitations like GPS accuracy but also on the method where the GPS location is taken in relation to the measured feature. If the methodology is known a maximum deviation from the measured point can be calculated and the encounter spot or feature may be related to the resulting circle using an instance of P171 at some place within. In more recent documentation often point coordinate information is provided that originates from GPS measurements or georeferencing from a map. This point coordinate information does not state the actual place of the encounter spot but tries to approximate it with a \u201cdeclarative\u201d place. The accuracy depends on the methodology used when creating the coordinates. It may be dependent on technical limitations like GPS accuracy but also on the method where the GPS location is taken in relation to the measured feature. If the methodology is known a maximum deviation from the measured point can be calculated and the encounter spot or feature may be related to the resulting circle using an instance of P171 at some place within."}

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: {"id": "7feb8f23-8e32-450d-994a-41f373384b2e", "value": "This property associates an instance of E53 Place with the instance of E18 Physical Thing that determines a reference space for this instance of E53 Place by being at rest with respect to this reference space. The relative stability of form of an instance of E18 Physical Thing defines its default reference space. The reference space is not spatially limited to the referred thing. For example, a ship determines a reference space in terms of which other ships in its neighbourhood may be described. Larger constellations of matter, such as continental plates, may comprise many physical features that are at rest with them and define the same reference space."}

{"id": "c5ad7812-3a7d-401d-9f36-63b1900ed494", "value": "This property identifies an instance of E53 Place that falls wholly within the extent of another instance of E53 Place. It addresses spatial containment only and does not imply any relationship between things or phenomena occupying these places. This property is a part of the fully developed path from E93 Presence through P161 has spatial projection (is spatial projection of), E53 Place, P89 falls within (contains) to E53 Place. This property is transitive and reflexive."}

{"id": "23c1d470-7047-4779-8ad1-7ae1b42f2ccf", "value": "This symmetric property associates an instance of E53 Place with another instance of E53 Place geometrically overlapping it. It does not specify anything about the shared area. This property is purely spatial. It does not imply that phenomena that define, by their extent, places related by P121 overlaps with have ever covered a common area at the same time or even coexisted. In contrast, spatiotemporal overlaps described by P132 spatiotemporally overlaps are the total of areas simultaneously covered by the related spacetime volumes."}

{"id": "ed44eba6-a84a-4328-ae41-80c45974c524", "value": "This property links an area, i.e., an instance of E53 Place to the instance of E18 Physical Thing upon which it is found. This area may either be identified by a name, or by a geometry in terms of a coordinate system adapted to the shape of the respective instance of E18 Physical Thing. Typically, names identifying sections of physical objects are composed of the name of a kind of part and the name of the object itself, such as \u201cThe poop deck of H.M.S. Victory\u201d, which is composed of \u201cpoop deck\u201d and \u201cH.M.S. Victory\u201d."}

{"id": "61bfc2de-3508-485a-af48-effcd8d41487", "value": "A catch-all category for all period terms described as the Neolithic in Eastern Africa. This term generally refers to the presence of domestic plants and/or animals increased sedentism and the use of polished or ground stone tools among other markers. As the term varies in what dates and markers it refers to across different regions more specific terms should be used if possible - the dates added here refer to the maximal extents. 6000BCE - 500CE.While the term Neolithic was developed in reference to West Asia North Africa and Europe and so may have less utility while referring to Africa it is still used (and does have some parallels due to connections along the Nile). | The period is associated with the later Holocene spread of pastoralism (a way of life centred around the herding and management of livestock) throughout eastern Africa changing its socio-economic and natural landscapes. | The Elmentaitan is a group of sites identified by minimally decorated mica-tempered ceramics large blade production its own lithic tool styles nearly exclusive use of green obsidian from Mt Eburru sources cremation burials and settlement in highland areas. Settlement locations commonly on savanna/forest ecotone and open sites above 1900m and large settlements above 2600m. Removal of central incisors common: ca.3300-1200BP"}

{"id": "40dc4c30-69f6-4966-adbf-39fb253e5b1a", "value": "Description: Zampia tradition ceramics were recovered from the Zampia Tumulus Fields all sites of the Douentza complex and from within Wind\u00e9 Koroji Tumulus n\u00b05. On the basis of the single radiocarbon date available(see below) and the absence of chipped stone object at the sites the Zampia tradition would appear to be the lineal successor to the Wind\u00e9 Koroji tradition with which it shares many features. The Zampia ceramic tradition is distinguished from that of Wind\u00e9 Koroji by a marked increase in the use of cord-wrapped stick roulette (CSR) and a decrease in the employment of twisted and knotted twone roulettes (Table 1). Twine impressions and roulettes alond the lips of vessels also cease. Addtionally two new vessel shapes are added large open bowls with inwardly-thickned rims (fig. 5e-f) and a new less-restricted jar shape (fig. 5a). If anything the canon of the decor placement seems even more standardized than with Wind\u00e9 Koroji tradition. [description of ceramics]"}
{"id": "e86d1d09-f33f-4d7b-a707-ea9a1b3fda9c", "value": "Characterised by small bifacial foliates and points side and end-scrapers blades and geometric microliths."}

{"id": "48783679-9bf6-4316-bb1b-a14004610660", "value": "In Senegal the Paleolithic covers the period from 300000 to 13000BC. It is commonly defined as the age of carved stone and its cultures are located in four main areas: Dakar and its surroundings the Gambia River valley and the Niokolo-Koba Park the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 valley and the Senegal River valley. | The Evolved Palaeolithic dating from around 27000 to 13000 BC is widespread across Senegal. Characteristic tools are points (pedunculated and foliated) bifaces blades scrapers drills denticulated and foliated bifacial armatures."}

{"id": "32be75de-fb03-4b37-92cb-3dd3e3ad608b", "value": "The Middle Paleolithic is dated between 75 000 and 27 000 BC. It is distributed over a large part of Senegal (the Fal\u00e9m\u00e9 the Niokolo-Koba Park the Senegal River valley the Cape Verde Peninsula). Characterised by side-scrapers notches backed knives Levallois and Moustero\u00efd Facies. | In Senegal the Mousteroid is not very characteristic of the Mousterian of Europe. It is generally defined by a tooling on flakes (points scrapers denticulates notches back knives rarity of burins and absence of typical scrapers) with small bifaces. The Mousteroid is very visible in the Cape Verde Peninsula where a series of surface deposits have been identified: Bargny Diokoul Cap des biches Ravin de Mbeth S\u00e9bikotane etc."}

{"id": "f8bcb6c3-1d1e-4564-b029-b5635f5c6fda", "value": "Shallow wide-mouthed necked vessels and wide-mouthed jars are the most common forms. Mostly undecorated the main diagnostic feature is the use of raised notched applique ridges below the rim for decoration or handles. Notches may also be present around the outer lip. 1400-1750AD"}

{"id": "7fdb60ad-efeb-4f36-8800-bfef74285e39", "value": "Tall jars with simple rims and other guard-shaped vessels predominate. Decorated with twisted cord roulette motifs around the rim and in horizontal and vertical strips possibly imitating leather straps on milk guards. 900AD"}

{"id": "8fc0d280-6251-4e85-bb85-c130eac210a5", "value": "Generally thick walled and sand tempered with little or no mica inclusions. Restricted decoration around the rim in horizontal vertical and cross hatched incisions. 1100-1400AD"}
{"id": "ad2fd38e-3332-4756-a533-a0575f7cb530", "value": "Pottery has twisted string impressions in horizontal vertical and diagonal bands below rim 1650-1810 AD"}

{"id": "8a2aeafd-cba8-4e53-a209-169f705a7ac0", "value": "This Neolithic stream is characterised by macrolithism and microlithism cut on quartz and flint. Polished hematite axes and grinding material are also numerous. In general the tools reflect the abundance and diversity of the rocks used. The deposits also provide ceramics decorated with impressions and degreased with lateritic gravel chamotte sand and quartz."}

Its foundation is unclear but at the earliest happened in the early 17th century CE (O'Fahey estimates the mid-17th century CE). 1600CE - 1916CE"}
