{"id": "79fd042e-d165-40c2-8516-4a250452ab7a", "value": "Description: Description: The Kobadi tradition would appear to have been of an entirely fisher-hunter-gatherer economic orientation and has been documented in the Malian Sahara and throughout most of the Middle Niger and Niger bend area (e.g. Raimbault and Dutour 1989 Togola and Raimbault 1991 MacDonald and Van Neer 1994 MacDonald 1996b Raimbault 1996). {"id": "9c8fb1af-8cc1-4a36-b58c-63df6e355057", "value": "After the disappearance of the medieval Nubian kingdoms the following 500 years saw new kingdoms arise across the region the most important of which were the Funj Sultanate of Sinnar and the Sultanate of Darfur. Between and around these other smaller polities were developing for example in parts of Kordofan as well as in parts of southern Sudan. Within many riverine areas even if nominally controlled by the Funj local leadership was commonly in the hands of \u2018tribal\u2019 leaders often known as meks. As elsewhere within Sudanic Africa these kingdoms often had wide horizons they and their peripheries were increasingly tied into large-scale trading networks while also sharing wide ranging cultural ties forged through the spread of Islam. Use more specific type where known."}

{"id": "c3fe27da-82f1-4a09-a258-d299951ce55c", "value": "Tradition is a term describing the persistence in a given area over a period of time in individual attributes, artifact types, in this case ceramics, or technologies; a culture that exists for an extended period of time and usually over an extended area."}

{"id": "88eb11df-ce6f-4788-b53b-6aa6afcdb534", "value": "A clay-based product, usually divided into pottery (such as earthenware, stoneware, and faience) and porcelain (soft-paste, hard-paste, and bone china). Excavated ceramics can be used for relative dating to give an approximate date range for a site. Any relative dating technique requires accurate identification. Site occupation dates derived from excavated ceramics must be used with caution and preferably in conjunction with other sources of evidence. Example: In the MAEASaM Chronological Type, the Ceramic class is classified into 5 broad sub-categories. For example: eathernware (generally pertaining to hand-made or thrown clay vessels). Earthenware includes local pottery manufactured on-site but can also relate to earthenware that has been imported through trade networks or other historical events. In some cases, a particular temper used during the firing of vessels can be used as a distinguishable marker for a particular time period. For example, charcoal, grog, quartz, silcrete, shell, bone, etc."}

{"id": "067cce43-197b-4c01-ac48-bc776a1bae0d", "value": "The Neolithic of Khant dates from 4890 BC. Its culture is named after the site of Khant a group of several shell middens. Its material consists of lithic tools bone wood and ceramics decorated by impressions. The bone tools (fishing implements) constitute the most characteristic remains of this industry."}

{"id": "f4fe99c1-ab34-4340-a88b-a1b0fb77e36c", "value": "The Middle East and in particular Egypt and the Levant played an important part in the history of glass where it it is generally acknowledged to have been invented in Mesopotamia in the middle of the third millennium BC. Middle East glass beads are commonly referred to as Phoenician beads and are spread around the Mediterranean littoral. Innovative glass beadmaking techniques where initiated in the Helenistic times and persisted trhought the Roman Empire into the Byzantine-Coptic periods and until the end of the Easly Islamd Period. The most widespread of glass beads from the Middle East are small monochrome oblate segmented beads recovered from Europe Middle East and Africa. These beads date from about 300 BCE to about 1200 CE and were an important staple in the Asian Maritime Trade network. | Produced from about 300 BCE to around 1200 CE Middle Eastern segmented glass beads have been identified in Europe the Middle East and Africa and are characteristically small monochrome oblates. They are however scarce in the Asian martime bead trade possibly due to competition with the numerous Indo-Pacific beads."}

{"id": "4a28edb5-bcd4-4bcb-ba88-7966ce6323e8", "value": "A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to wooden structures or objects by the comparative study of the growth rings in trees and aged wood."}

{"id": "b463a8d9-dc07-49d3-aad4-fded8d45a81b", "value": "Residential land uses range from high density, represented by the multiple-unit structures of urban cores, to low density, where houses are on lots of more than an acre, on the periphery of urban expansion."}

{"id": "236b9728-19b5-4ded-b9bc-bc4fa9c1d1b4", "value": "L'utilisation des sols \u00e0 des fins r\u00e9sidentielles va de la haute densit\u00e9, repr\u00e9sent\u00e9e par les structures \u00e0 logements multiples des centres urbains, \u00e0 la faible densit\u00e9, o\u00f9 les maisons sont situ\u00e9es sur des terrains de plus d'un acre, \u00e0 la p\u00e9riph\u00e9rie de l'expansion urbaine."}

{"id": "6b20f389-b7a2-48de-a239-579a297585d2", "value": "The Sultanate of Ifat was a medieval Sunni Muslim state between the late 13th century and early 15th century. Led by the Walashma dynasty it absorbed the Sultanate of Shewa."}
{"id": "c1a6a700-a29d-4df3-a78f-91921ced3d41", "value": "A small Christian kingdom based at Jebel Adda whose rulers until c.1365 were lesser kings under broader rule of the kingdom of Makuria."}

{"id": "e209576a-6516-4cac-9194-e053d1946a77", "value": "Description: This tradition has been recovered from every site associated by (p.39) oral tradition with the historical state of Segou. Its range of rim forms is limited (only everted thickened rims and pot lids) and its range of decoration is almost entirely different from Pre-Segovian assemblages. Likewise the paste of the Segou pottery tradition though also of tempered grog is relatively coarse with the common addition of small lateritic pebbles. Date range: 1600 CE - 1861CE. | ~1700 CE - 1861 CE"}

{"id": "ab8d34fd-8038-463a-8ede-92d9e4ec1710", "value": "A broader term applied from the Eurasian Three Age System to Sudan (due to connections with Egypt along the Nile). Characterised primarily by the presence of bronze metallurgy as well as other changes variable on specific subregions. Dates given are widest possible for whole area - they vary across regions. 3700BCE - 1450BCE. | A broader term for the Bronze Age period within Lower Nubia generally split into the A-Group and C-Group cultural phases - the formerly defined B-Group phase has been since called into question. 3700BCE - 1550 BCE | The first cultural phase generally recognised for the Bronze Age of Lower Nubia. Cultivated various domestic plants and maintained domesticated sheep goats and cattle as well as hunting gathering and fishing. Some pottery styles similar to both Egypt in the North and to Upper Nubia in the South as well as a distinct eggshell ware. Most excavation so far has focused on burials with the period particularly characterised by flexed position burials with varying grave goods. Group suddenly disappears shortly after the unification of Egypt and there is limited evidence for occupation of the area before the C-Group is visible. 3700-2800BC | A sub-period of the A-Group as based mainly on the chronology of Egyptian artefacts found within A-Group assemblages (as a result of which it is problematic and unclear). The Classic/Middle A-Group is contemporary with Naqada IId2-IIIa2. 3250BCE - 3150BCE"}

{"id": "b92a008c-c471-4b38-a8af-88bb20bde6ed", "value": "Marked by the appearance of Azanian pottery: triangular oblique and double zig-zag patterns predominating also Sassanian Islamic glass and carnelian beads and Roman Amphora 300-600CE"}

{"id": "6252746d-31bd-4394-b723-939d4aeb0f0c", "value": "Oral traditions claimed Payoungou and Korop was originally founded by the Bainouk: excavations have shown that human occupation of the site does indeed pre-date Kaabu. Four units yielded pre-Kaabu deposits: PYG-A PYG-C PYG-D PYG-E and KRP-E verifed through a combination of radiocarbon dates and pottery traits."}

{"id": "f888809d-a2cc-47a5-a598-8c1013aeb321", "value": "This facies dating between 3584 and 2919 BC includes several deposits located on the Ogolian dunes of western Senegal. Microlithics are the most characteristic material which are also associated with ceramicstempered with sand."}

{"id": "af563c10-3cf6-455e-9fec-1e9571324bb1", "value": "Marked by statistically diverse local pottery spindle whorls coins portable stoves and lamps chlorite schist Islamic monochromes Chinese Longquan and Tongan ware Indonesian Sawankholok or Sisatchanalai jars indo-Pacific beads and Egyptian glass signalling trade with China Southeast Asia India and the Persian Gulf 1250-1500CE"}

{"id": "6ea19023-2a79-4843-adfd-102772161e40", "value": "Formations where trees in the various storeys and the undergrowth cover a high proportion (> 40 percent) of the ground and do not have a continuous dense grass layer (cf. the following definition). They are either managed or unmanaged forests, primary or in advanced state of reconstitution and may have been logged-over one or more times, having kept their characteristics of forest stands, possibly with modified structure and composition. Typical examples of tropical closed forest formations include tropical rain forest and mangrove forest."}

{"id": "dd77cd54-5b01-4708-a47b-39d459a95af4", "value": "Formations o\u00f9 les arbres des diff\u00e9rents \u00e9tages et le sous-bois couvrent une forte proportion (> 40 pour cent) du sol et ne pr\u00e9sentent pas de couche herbeuse dense et continue (cf. la d\u00e9finition suivante). Il s'agit de for\u00eats g\u00e9r\u00e9es ou non, primaires ou en phase avanc\u00e9e de reconstitution, qui peuvent avoir \u00e9t\u00e9 exploit\u00e9es une ou plusieurs fois, tout en conservant leurs caract\u00e9ristiques de peuplements forestiers, avec \u00e9ventuellement une structure et une composition modifi\u00e9es. La for\u00eat tropicale humide et la for\u00eat de mangrove sont des exemples typiques de formations foresti\u00e8res tropicales ferm\u00e9es.\n\nTraduit avec www.DeepL.com/Translator (version gratuite)"}

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: {"id": "d5c708fd-51bc-433a-989d-7e47abf96c19", "value": "Blade Tool Tradition Phase B (Ethiopian Rift Valley)"}
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: {"id": "6c383f8d-4ff9-4bc0-b2a7-9a95a08faff7", "value": "Based on Brandt (1980) and Clark and Williams (1978) classification of the Ethiopian Blade Tool Tradition phase B is defined by the increase in frequency of microlithic material including the manufacture of burims and awls. Note that this industry has been classified based on research that has been conducted in and around Lake Besaka Rift Valley Ethiopia Date range: c. 11 - 5 kya."}

{"id": "5f43070a-e2ed-4974-85ab-c197af4a79bd", "value": "Regional subtradition of the Pastoral Neolithic the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic (SPN) encompasses sites with a predominately domestic fauna associated with a wide range of ceramic styles including Narosura Nderit Ileret Akira and Maringishu a preference for grey-hued obsidians sourced to the Lake Naivasha Basin particular lithic production techniques and tool styles cairn burials and settlement in highland and lowland savannas. 5000-1300BP | Sites found in central Kenya to northern Tanzania in areas above 1500m asl. 3300-1300BP | This pottery tradition has ceramics associated with stone bowls pestles axes cattle- and caprine-based economies as well as diverse stone artefacts and large settlements dating to 2nd millennium BCE and 10th century CE around the Central Rift south to Eyasi east to Tsavo (coastal hinterland) and the Serengeti-Mara Plains. 1900-1200BP"}

{"id": "d802b100-80ab-4ba1-9c0b-cf81151fb689", "value": "This phase marks an important break in the history of Wanar. Pottery with lids on jars are abandoned in favour of small containers. The appearance of vases, made by the coil method, correspond with the appearance of short monolithic stone monuments and ritual practices."}
